candidate_findings.message: test_send_request_to_llm never calls send_request_to_llm. It awaits the mocked send_request_to_open_ai directly, so the test passes no matter what the real chat function does and covers none of its logic. Line 41 is `await chat_interface.send_request_to_open_ai(...)`, and line 24 patches that same name with an AsyncMock whose side_effect returns `("", [["Hello","Hi there!"]], "video_path.mp4")`. The real `send_request_to_llm` (chat/interface.py:77-94) builds the system prompt, joins on history, dispatches to elevenlabs or zonos, and appends to CHAT_HISTORY. None of that code runs.

Every assertion checks a value the test's own mock produced, so the test is a tautology: it cannot fail on a wrong implementation, and it says nothing about the real CHAT_HISTORY behaviour. `llm_side_effect` (lines 20-22) does `CHAT_HISTORY.append(["Hello", "Hi there!"])` and returns the tuple that lines 47-51 then assert on (`first_llm_answer[0] == ""`, `len(CHAT_HISTORY) == 1`, `CHAT_HISTORY[0] == ["Hello","Hi there!"]`). The real append at interface.py:93 is never reached.

The test depends on the pytest-mock (`mocker`) and pytest-asyncio (`@pytest.mark.asyncio`) plugins, which the project does not declare. On the project's own environment it errors with a missing fixture, or the async test is not run. pyproject.toml's dev group lists only `pytest` and `pytest-cov`. poetry.lock has no `name = "pytest-mock"` or `name = "pytest-asyncio"` package entry; those names appear only as other packages' extras. The test takes a `mocker` argument and is an `async def` marked `@pytest.mark.asyncio`.

The test calls the real `_load_avatar_infos_for_chat`, not the patched one. It opens the developer's real TinyDB at DB_PATH (creating the file if it is missing) and crashes with AttributeError when no avatar page settings row exists. Line 8 does `from aafactory.chat.interface import _load_avatar_infos_for_chat`, which binds the name locally before line 31 patches `aafactory.chat.interface._load_avatar_infos_for_chat`, so the patch does not affect it. The real function (interface.py:55-60) runs `TinyDB(DB_PATH)` with DB_PATH = ROOT_DIR/databases/avatar_db.json (configuration.py:8), then `avatar_page_settings_table.get(doc_id=1).get("avatar_name")`, which raises on None in a fresh DB. tests/test_configuration.py defines a TEST_DB_PATH that this test does not use.

The test never asserts that the patched send_request_to_generate_video or send_request_to_open_ai were called, or with what arguments. It also passes ten positional arguments to a function whose real signature takes one `messages` list, so the mocks can drift from reality unnoticed. There is no `assert_called*` anywhere in the file. The `send_request_to_generate_video` mock is never used. Line 41 calls `send_request_to_open_ai(avatar_info[9], "Hello", ...)` with 10 args, while interface.py:86 calls it as `send_request_to_open_ai(messages)`.

The code under test has defects that the new test was meant to cover and cannot catch. The previous user message is string-concatenated onto the new prompt instead of being sent as history, and an unknown voice_model leaves `audio_response` unbound, so line 91 raises UnboundLocalError. Line 81 is `user_message = CHAT_HISTORY[-1][0] + user_prompt`, which joins only the last user text with no separator and drops assistant turns. Lines 87-91 assign `audio_response` only in the `elevenlabs`/`zonos` branches, then use it unconditionally. The new test mocks around send_request_to_llm and never exercises either path.

The test clears the module-global CHAT_HISTORY at the start but never restores it, so state leaks into any later test that touches chat history. Line 14 calls `CHAT_HISTORY.clear()`, and then the side effect appends to the global list (line 21). There is no fixture teardown or monkeypatch of CHAT_HISTORY.

The test calls its own mock instead of send_request_to_llm, so broken chat orchestration will still pass. Lines 18–22 replace send_request_to_open_ai with llm_side_effect, and line 35 calls that replacement directly. The side effect supplies every asserted return value and appends the asserted history itself; the production send_request_to_llm never executes.

The avatar-loader patch misses the imported reference, leaving the test dependent on the real application database. Line 2 imports _load_avatar_infos_for_chat directly, while line 26 patches only chat_interface._load_avatar_infos_for_chat. Line 33 invokes the original imported function, which opens TinyDB(DB_PATH) and calls avatar_page_settings.get without checking whether the settings record exists; an empty database therefore causes an AttributeError before the assertions.

The new test requires undeclared pytest plugins and cannot run with the project's declared development dependencies. The test requests the mocker fixture and uses pytest.mark.asyncio, requiring pytest-mock and pytest-asyncio. pyproject.toml declares only pytest and pytest-cov as development dependencies, and neither required plugin has a package entry in poetry.lock. A clean project installation cannot provide the mocker fixture.

The User Guide still says notes are not saved and cannot be undone, but this change makes them both saved and undoable, so the guide now tells users the wrong thing. UserGuide.md:335 still reads "Records a date-bound note that will be persisted in future milestones. Currently, it validates syntax via CLI and confirms receipt." Line 360 still reads "`note` is not undoable yet because it currently validates input and shows a confirmation message without persisting data." The diff only changed the example on line 340. Meanwhile NoteCommand.execute now calls model.setNote and isStateMutating() returns true, and JsonSerializableAddressBook now writes the notes map to the data file.

AddressBook.removeNote is dead code: no Model method, command or parser calls it, while the User Guide still documents a `note d-/DATE` delete command that does not exist. AddressBook.removeNote(VisitDate) is new, but Model/ModelManager add only setNote and getPlannerNoteProperty. NoteCommandParser tokenizes only PREFIX_NAME and PREFIX_DATE and rejects input unless both are present. NoteCommand.MESSAGE_USAGE dropped the "Delete format: d-/DATE" line, but UserGuide.md:342-349 and the summary table at line 439 still advertise `note d-/2026-03-24`. Only AddressBookTest.removeNote_* calls the method.

Recording a note for a date that already has one silently replaces the old note, yet the message still says "New note recorded", so the user is not told that text was lost. NoteCommand.execute calls model.setNote(date, noteContent), and AddressBook.setNote calls notes.put(date, note), which overwrites any existing value. VisitDate subclasses compare by value (OneTimeDate.equals compares the LocalDate), so `d/2026-03-24` and `d/24/3/26` hit the same key. MESSAGE_SUCCESS is always "New note recorded: %1$s". `undo` can bring the old note back, but only one level of undo exists.

Notes are stored in a HashMap, so their insertion order is lost on save and reload; after a restart the planner may show combined notes for a day (e.g. an everyday note plus a dated note) in a different order than before. `private final Map<String, String> notes = new HashMap<>();` collects the notes, and toModelType loops over notes.entrySet() to call addressBook.setNote. AddressBook keeps a LinkedHashMap, and ModelManager.updatePlannerNote joins notes in map order with "\n\n". The test updatePlannerNote_multipleNotes_mergesNotes comments "Use LinkedHashMap in AddressBook to ensure order", which shows the order was meant to be kept.

The planner joins all of a day's notes into one block of text with no date label, so the user cannot tell which note belongs to which date rule (everyday, weekly, yearly or one-off). updatePlannerNote appends entry.getValue().toString() for every key where isOn(currentPlannedDate) is true, separated by "\n\n", wraps the result in a new NoteContent and shows it as one NoteCard. The VisitDate key is dropped. NoteContent.VALIDATION_REGEX was changed to "(?s)[^\\s].*" just so this joined text passes validation.

The new tests don't cover the behaviours this change most needs to protect: undoing and redoing a note, the planner panel reacting to note changes, and rejecting bad notes in the data file. One assertion is also too weak to catch a wrong starting state. setNote_updatesPlannerNote only checks `assertFalse(note.equals(initialPlannerNote))`; it would also pass if the initial value were some other non-null note. No test runs NoteCommand and then undoState/redoState, even though isStateMutating() is now true. No test covers the PlannerListPanel listener. JsonSerializableAddressBookTest adds no case for an invalid date key or a blank or null note value, so the new IllegalValueException branches in toModelType are untested.

The diff adds tests for code the note feature never touches, which pads coverage without testing the change. LogicManagerTest.getMethods_success checks getAddressBook, getAddressBookFilePath, getGuiSettings and getTheme. ModelManagerTest adds discardState_clearsPendingState, commitState_noPendingState_noChange and equals_differentTypes_returnsFalse. None of these exercise notes or the planner note property.

Replacing notes with the address book’s own read-only view silently deletes every note. getNoteMap() returns Collections.unmodifiableMap(notes), a live view. Calling setNotes(book.getNoteMap()), resetData(book), or model.setAddressBook(model.getAddressBook()) reaches this.notes.clear() before putAll(notes), so the source map is already empty.

The user guide incorrectly says notes are neither persisted nor undoable. Lines 335 and 360 describe confirmation-only behavior and explicitly deny undo support. NoteCommand.execute now calls model.setNote(), isStateMutating() returns true, and LogicManager saves the address book after execution; JsonSerializableAddressBook now serializes notes.

The Rust benchmark never calls the converted function, so the reported Rust time and the 'Rust is Nx faster' speedup measure an empty loop rather than the conversion. _RUST_BENCH_TEMPLATE times a loop whose body is `// {fn_lower}({call_args});  // uncomment once the Rust signature is known` followed by `std::hint::black_box(&{first_array});`. run_benchmark then computes `speedup = fortran_ms / rust_ms` (line 326), and BenchResult.summary prints 'Rust is {ratio:.2f}x faster than Fortran'. That figure goes into the report and the CLI summary table.

The accuracy check reports a function as passed when no numerical comparison ran (no Rust binary, crate build failed, or length mismatch), so the report shows ✅ accuracy for code that was never checked. When `errors` is empty, run_accuracy_check returns `AccuracyResult(passed=fortran_ok_count > 0, ...)`, so a Fortran-only run counts as a pass. Line 676 also returns `passed=True` when no routine or source is given. convert.py and cli.py are called with `crate_dir if build_ok else None`, so a failed cargo build sends every function down this path. convert.py prints `"✅" if acc.passed` and reporter.py renders `✅` in the accuracy table.

For Fortran FUNCTIONs that take array arguments (ddot, dasum, dnrm2, idamax, …), the Rust and Fortran drivers print their values in different orders, so the element-wise comparison lines up the wrong values and reports errors for a correct translation. In generate_fortran_driver the array print loops are added first and the result is appended last (`print_lines.append(f"      WRITE(*,'{print_fmt}') {result_var}")`, line 471). _RUST_EXAMPLE_TEMPLATE_FN prints `_result` first and the arrays after (`println!("{{:.15e}}", _result as f64);` then `{rust_prints}`). Both outputs have the same length, so run_accuracy_check compares `rust_out[i]` against `fortran_out[i]` across shifted positions.

The default strategy (3) passes f2c's C statements through unchanged into the Rust body, so the generated code does not compile wherever f2c is installed (it is installed in the devcontainer). The result is still marked a successful conversion. _translate_c_line falls through to `return s + "  // TODO: verify"` for every C statement it does not recognise. f2c output such as `a_dim1 = *lda;` or `c__[i__ + j * c_dim1] = 0.;` is emitted verbatim inside `pub unsafe fn`, with i32/&mut [f64] parameters. convert() then sets `success=True` (line 100) without running any compile check, even though the module docstring promises 'Run cargo check and report results'. A single broken module fails `cargo build` for the whole crate.

The LLM strategies report success even when the code still fails to compile after the repair rounds, so the report shows '✅ OK' for broken output. LLMFirstStrategy.convert returns `ConversionResult(..., success=True, ...)` whether or not the final `quick_check` passed; it only prints 'Could not fully compile…'. AgenticStrategy.convert does the same (agentic.py line 143) and then runs `polish_unsafe_rust` after the compile loop (line 135) without compiling again, so the final source was never checked.

The GitHub token found automatically (via `gh auth token` or the Copilot hosts.json) is sent as a Bearer header to whatever LLM_BASE_URL says, and that value can come from a `.env` in the current directory. Running the tool inside an untrusted checkout can therefore send the user's GitHub token to an attacker's endpoint. _resolve_api_key returns `_load_token_from_gh_cli()` / `_load_token_from_vscode_store()` for provider github_models (line 142). `self.base_url = base_url or os.environ.get("LLM_BASE_URL") or self._default_url()` is not restricted to the provider's endpoint. _load_dotenv and convert.py both load `.env` from the CWD, and chat() posts with `headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self.api_key}"`.

Fortran sources are downloaded over plain HTTP, and from an unpinned `master` branch, then compiled and executed by gfortran and sent to the LLM. Someone who can tamper with the network or the upstream can inject code that runs on the host or instructions that reach the model. `_NETLIB_BASE = "http://www.netlib.org/blas/"`, `_BLAS_TARBALL = "http://www.netlib.org/blas/blas-3.11.0.tgz"`, and `_LAPACK_BLAS_GITHUB_RAW = ".../lapack/master/BLAS/SRC/"`, with no hash check. _compile_run_fortran and _run_fortran_bench compile and run the fetched files, and the strategies pass `routine.source` into the LLM prompts.

LLM output is written into the crate, compiled, and executed by the accuracy and benchmark binaries without human review or sandboxing. A prompt injection in the source the model reads could cause host code to run. scaffold_crate writes `r.rust_source` (the model's reply after _strip_fences) straight into `src/{mod}.rs`. build_crate, test_crate and _compile_run_rust_example then run `cargo build`/`cargo test` and execute the example binary with the user's privileges.

The path-traversal guard on tarball extraction does not handle symlink or hardlink members, so a malicious tarball (fetched over HTTP) can still write outside output_dir. _try_download_tarball checks only that `(output_dir / member.name).resolve()` lies under output_dir, then calls `t.extractall(output_dir, members=safe_members)` with no `filter='data'` and no check of `member.issym()/islnk()` or `linkname`.

convert.py's own `.env` loader keeps surrounding quotes and runs before LLMClient's loader, so a quoted `LLM_API_KEY="…"` is stored with the quotes and authentication fails. At module import, convert.py does `os.environ.setdefault(_key.strip(), _val.strip())` with no quote stripping. llm_client._load_dotenv does strip quotes, but it skips any key already in os.environ (`if key and key not in os.environ`), so the quoted value wins.

Strategy 2's 'Questioner LLM' is a fixed list of keyword-triggered questions rather than an LLM, unlike what the README and strategy description say. _generate_questions builds `questions` from `if "LSAME" in routine.source.upper()`, `if "IMPLICIT" not in ...` and similar checks, with no LLM call. The README says 'Questioner LLM asks up to 3 clarifying questions'.

The hybrid strategy's LLM polish output is used without removing markdown fences, so a reply wrapped in ```rust fences produces a .rs file that does not compile. `polished = self.llm.polish_unsafe_rust(...)`; `if polished.strip(): rust_source = polished`. The other strategies pass the same call through `_strip_fences`.

The README marks Milestone 1 (full automation of dgemm in all three strategies) as done and calls the output a 'ready-to-use crate', but the code does not support either claim. `- [x] Milestone 1 — Automate dgemm conversion (all three strategies)`. Meanwhile the hybrid path emits uncompilable or TODO-stub bodies (`// TODO: translate from Fortran source`), and the Rust benchmark call is commented out.

About 3,000 lines of new pipeline code were added with no tests at all; the README defers them to later. The export contains no test files (no tests/ directory or test_*.py). README says `# Run the test suite (once tests are added)` / `# pytest`. The harness logic that decides pass/fail (run_accuracy_check, _fortran_call, parse_arg_declarations) has no unit coverage.

Three new runtime dependencies are never imported, and every dependency is unpinned (`>=`), which widens the supply-chain surface for no benefit. requirements.txt and setup.py list `click>=8.1.0`, `colorama>=0.4.6` and `fparser>=0.2.1`; grepping the package finds no import of click, colorama or fparser.

The devcontainer installs Rust by piping an unpinned remote script into sh and updates the toolchain on every start, so builds cannot be reproduced and tool versions change silently. `RUN curl ... https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --profile minimal`, and devcontainer.json has `"postStartCommand": "rustup update stable --no-self-update 2>/dev/null || true"`.

The 429 handling sleeps for whatever Retry-After the server sends, with no upper limit, and each 429 uses up a retry. Run after run can stall, and the final error message reads 'None'. `wait = int(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", "5")); time.sleep(wait); continue` has no cap. After all attempts end in 429, `last_exc` is still None in `raise LLMError(f"... {last_exc}")`.

generate_report opens a browser by default, including in the `--non-interactive` CI mode. `open_browser: bool = True`, then `webbrowser.open(html_path.as_uri())`. convert.py's _run_non_interactive calls generate_report without passing `open_browser=False`.

The '10-function sample' takes the first N Level-1 routines instead of the curated BLAS_SAMPLE, so the sample never includes dgemm. Several helpers are dead code. _parse_sample_input returns `BLAS_FUNCTIONS[:n]`. `BLAS_SAMPLE`, `topological_order`, `clippy_crate` and `add_rust_tests` are defined but never referenced.

The documented provider names disagree: the devcontainer and convert.py's docstring use 'copilot' as the default, while llm_client says github_models. `"containerEnv": {"LLM_PROVIDER": "copilot"}` and convert.py's docstring has `LLM_PROVIDER copilot | openai | openai_compatible (default: copilot)`, whereas llm_client.py's default is `"github_models"` and treats copilot as a legacy alias.

The Rust benchmark never calls the converted routine, so reported speedups compare Fortran computation with an empty Rust loop. The generated benchmark comments out `{fn_lower}({call_args})` and only executes `black_box(&{first_array})`; run_benchmark nevertheless divides the Fortran timing by this timing and reports it as speedup.

Accuracy checks report success when Rust fails to build or no numerical comparison completes. When the Fortran reference runs but crate_dir is None, Rust compilation fails, or output lengths differ, errors remains empty and run_accuracy_check returns passed=fortran_ok_count > 0. A mocked reference returning [1.0] with crate_dir=None reproduced passed=True and failed_cases=0. The reporter displays this as a successful accuracy result.

The offline fallback generates empty function bodies rather than conversions while reporting conversion success. With f2c unavailable and no LLM key, convert calls _direct_fortran_to_rust, which emits the source only as comments and returns a constant for functions; convert unconditionally sets success=True. DGEMM therefore leaves C unchanged rather than computing alpha*A*B + beta*C.

The f2c conversion path preserves C syntax and unmatched braces, producing invalid Rust for ordinary f2c output. _build_unsafe_rust opens a Rust function, then copies the C body's opening and closing braces through _translate_c_line before appending another closing brace. It also passes through C pointer expressions, labels and return values without valid Rust translation. With f2c installed and no LLM, this output is packaged directly.

Function accuracy checks compare return values against array elements because the two drivers print outputs in different orders. For a function with array arguments such as DDOT, generate_fortran_driver appends the function result after array print loops, while _RUST_EXAMPLE_TEMPLATE_FN prints _result before rust_prints. Equal-length streams are compared positionally, so a correct translation fails.

Continued Fortran routine headers lose all arguments, breaking generated signatures and test drivers. parse_source calls _extract_args on the first header line alone; _ARG_LIST requires the closing parenthesis on that line. Parsing `SUBROUTINE FOO(A,` followed by a fixed-form continuation `+ B)` reproduced args=[]. Subsequent hybrid conversion and driver generation use this empty list.

Failed compile-repair loops still mark the routine as successfully converted. When quick_check fails on all three attempts, or repair raises after a failed check, convert still returns success=True. AgenticStrategy likewise returns success=True and additionally replaces the checked source with an unchecked polish result. The CLI and report derive conversion status from this flag.

The installed console command may fail because its target module is omitted from the package. The entry point targets convert:main, but setup declares only packages=find_packages() and no py_modules=['convert']; convert.py is a top-level module outside those packages. A wheel installation outside the checkout therefore lacks the entry point's target.

Model-generated Rust executes with the caller's filesystem, network access and credentials without an isolation boundary. LLM strategies pass returned Rust directly into scaffold_crate; cargo test runs its generated tests and _compile_run_rust_example executes a binary calling the generated function through subprocess.run. A model response containing filesystem reads or network requests in that function executes automatically during the normal pipeline; cargo check supplies no security validation or sandbox.

On the GET download route, the unvalidated `download_language` query value now reaches the backend as both the Accept-Language header and the `lang` query parameter. A crafted or unsupported value can make every download request fail, or send the backend a locale it doesn't expect. On GET, `download_language = (req.query.download_language?.toString() || req.language) as Locale` is cast but never checked; `downloadLanguageValidator()` only runs in the POST branch. Before this change `fetch` overwrote it with `queryParams.set('lang', this.lang)`. Now `downloadPublishedData`/`downloadPublishedPivotData` pass `lang: language as Locale` (consumer-api.ts:228/241), and fetch puts it in `'Accept-Language': lang` and `queryParams.set('lang', lang)`. For example, `?download_language=xx` is forwarded to the backend as is, and a value with characters that aren't valid in a header makes `fetch` throw. That error gets wrapped as UnknownException.

The publisher preview download has the same gap: `download_language` from the GET query isn't validated and now flows into the authenticated backend request's Accept-Language header and `lang` parameter. `const download_language = (req.query.download_language?.toString() || req.language) as Locale;` is passed to `req.pubapi.downloadDatasetPreview(...)`, which now calls `this.fetch({ ..., lang: language as Locale })` (publisher-api.ts:932). PublisherApi.fetch sets `'Accept-Language': lang` next to the `Authorization: Bearer` header, and `queryParams.set('lang', lang)`. The validator only runs on POST.

`language as Locale` hides a type mismatch: the methods still take `language: string`, so the compiler can't catch a non-Locale value being passed in. `downloadPublishedData(..., language: string)` followed by `lang: language as Locale`. The same pattern appears at consumer-api.ts:241 and publisher-api.ts:932. The callers already hold a `Locale`-typed value, so the parameter could be typed `Locale` without any cast.

Only one end-to-end case covers the fix: the consumer, unfiltered, non-pivot CSV. Pivot downloads and the publisher preview download also changed but have no test showing they honour the chosen language. The new `CSV Download Language Content` test submits only `viewType: 'unfiltered'` (no pivot axes), so it exercises `downloadPublishedData` only. Nothing exercises `downloadPublishedPivotData` or `PublisherApi.downloadDatasetPreview`, both of which this diff changed.

No unit test checks that the request URL carries the download language rather than the UI language, even though the existing unit suite already asserts request URLs such as `?lang=en`. The fix is therefore guarded only by a slow e2e test that depends on fixture data. tests/publisher-api.test.ts asserts exact fetch URLs ending in `lang=en` for other methods, but there is no case for `downloadDatasetPreview`, and no consumer-api unit test for `downloadPublishedData` with `cy-GB` on an English-UI client. The only new test is the Playwright spec, which relies on the e2e fixture's `' - CY'` suffix (tests-e2e/publish/helpers/publishing-steps.ts:336).

Several 'not applicable' branches use `break` where they mean `continue`, so the first such record silently ends the whole `for record in data` loop and every record after it is dropped from the knowledge graph. `break` sits directly inside `for record in data:` (line 135) at lines 413 (Allosteric modulator, Action 'Neutral' or None), 530 (Antagonist, 'Partial agonist'), 710 (Fusion protein, 'Binding'), 925 (Type None, 'Binding'/'Competitive') and 1063 (Subunit-specific, 'Mixed'). The function then reaches `return [KnowledgeGraph(nodes=nodes, edges=edges)]` (line 1094) holding only the records processed so far. Each case only does `print("not applicable")` (stdout, not koza.log), so nothing records the truncation.

The action lists spell 'Agnoist' instead of 'Agonist', so Agonist-type records whose Action is 'Agonist' (and Allosteric modulator/Agonist records) now produce no edges at all. `agnoist_list_with_separate_directly_physically_interacts_with_edge = ['Activation', 'Agnoist', ...]` (line 257). The `elif record["Action"] == "Agonist"` arm inside that block can never be reached. The diff deleted the old `if record["Type"] == 'Agonist' and record["Action"] != "Binding"` fallback and added no `not in` branch for Agonist, so these records hit no branch. The same misspelling at line 331 drops Allosteric modulator/'Agonist' records.

Because of the same 'Agnoist' typo, Activator/Agonist records fall into the fallback branch, which no longer sets a causal mechanism for 'Agonist', so they are emitted with causal_mechanism_qualifier None and without the directly_physically_interacts_with edge. Line 167's list holds 'Agnoist'. The fallback at line 217 (`not in activator_list...`) only handles 'Activation', None, 'Positive' and 'Potentiation'. The diff removed the `elif record["Action"] == "Agonist": ... agonism` arm from that branch.

Types that used to map every action now emit nothing for any action missing from their new allowlist (Antagonist, Antibody, Channel blocker, Gating inhibitor, Fusion protein, Allosteric modulator), so source records are dropped silently with no log. Before the change, `if record["Type"] == 'Antagonist' and record["Action"] != "Binding"`, `if record["Type"] == 'Antibody':`, `if record["Type"] == 'Channel blocker':` and `if record["Type"] == 'Gating inhibitor':` covered all actions. Now each is gated by `record["Action"] in <type>_list...` (lines 476, 571, 639, 699, 757) and has no `not in` counterpart.

`predicate` now defaults to the string "None" rather than None. In the Type-None and Subunit-specific fallback branches, an action without its own arm builds a ChemicalAffectsGeneAssociation with predicate "None", which either fails validation or writes an invalid predicate. Line 138 sets `predicate = "None"`. The diff removed the old per-type `predicate = BIOLINK_AFFECTS` from the Type-None and Subunit-specific blocks. In the fallback at line 1059, an Action other than 'Mixed' or 'Potentiation' (for example None) leaves predicate as "None" when line 1076 passes it as `predicate = predicate`. The Type-None fallback (lines 966 onward) has the same gap for actions other than None and 'Potentiation'.

The Endogenous check compares against the exact string "TRUE", so if the CSV stores the flag in another form ('true', 't', 'True' or a bool), every edge silently stays affects/increased and regulates/upregulated is never used. `if record["Endogenous"] == "TRUE":` (line 159), with no normalisation of the value anywhere in prepare() or the transform. Nothing in the repo (yaml or tests) records what form the value takes in the CSV.

The new aggregation groups on columns that can be NaN ('Type', 'Action', 'Endogenous') under pandas' default `dropna=True`. Any row with a missing value in those keys may be dropped before the transform, which would leave every `record["Action"] is None` branch dead. `source_subset_df.groupby(group_cols, as_index=False)` with `group_cols = ['Target', 'Target UniProt ID', 'Ligand ID', 'Ligand', 'Type', 'Action', 'Endogenous']` and no `dropna=False`. The transform still branches on `record["Action"] is None` and `record["Type"] is None` (for example lines 224 and 920).

Fusion protein/Inhibition records are now tagged molecular_channel_blockage instead of inhibition, which looks like a copy-paste from the Channel blocker block. Line 699 onward first sets `causal_mechanism_qualifier = CausalMechanismQualifierEnum.inhibition`, then the 'Inhibition' arm overrides it with `CausalMechanismQualifierEnum.molecular_channel_blockage` (line 712). Before the change, this path used `inhibition`.

The change rewrites the mapping for every Type/Action combination, adds aggregation and the Endogenous switch, and adds no tests, so none of the defects above is caught. A search of tests/ for 'gtopdb' matches only tests/unit/ingests/dgidb/test_dgidb.py. The diff touches only gtopdb.py and gtopdb_rig.yaml.

The yaml-language-server schema header is written inside a double-quoted PowerShell string, so PowerShell expands `$schema` as an undefined variable. Every generated manifest gets the broken header `# yaml-language-server: =https://...` instead of the schema reference the change says the winget-pkgs pipeline requires. Lines 209, 222 and 243 are `@("# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://aka.ms/winget-manifest.version.1.12.0.schema.json", ...` in a `shell: pwsh` step. In an expandable (double-quoted) string `$schema` is a variable reference that ends at `=`, and nothing assigns `$schema`. The text therefore never contains `$schema=`. The comment at lines 201-204 says the pipeline 'fails manifest validation' without this header, so every 'Submit to winget' run still uploads manifests that fail. A single-quoted string or an escaped `` `$schema `` is needed.
