The change says it prevents ReDoS, but it only caps the length of the pattern and the input. A short pattern with catastrophic backtracking passes validation, and running it against a few dozen characters still blocks the single-threaded MCP server. The only new runtime guard is `if (pattern.pattern.length > MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH)` before `new RegExp(pattern.pattern, safeFlags)` and `regex.exec(line)`. There is no timeout, no check for nested quantifiers, no worker isolation and no per-line length limit. Trigger: `add_custom_rule` with pattern `(a+)+$` (6 chars) gets through `validatePattern`, because it compiles and is under 1 000 chars. Then `execute_custom_rules` with code `'a'.repeat(40)+'!'` (far under 500 000) makes `regex.exec` backtrack exponentially. Even so, CHANGELOG.md line 36 says the caps are "preventing ReDoS attacks (#127)".

The size guard runs `stat` without checking that the path is a regular file. A character device, FIFO or procfs entry reports size 0, passes the check, and is then read with no bound, so the 'capped before reading' promise can be bypassed and memory exhausted. `getFileStats` calls `fs.promises.stat(filePath)` (fileUtils.ts:157), and the handler checks only `stats.size > MAX_FILE_SIZE_BYTES` before `code = await readFile(path)`, which is `fs.promises.readFile(filePath, 'utf-8')` with no length limit. Trigger: `execute_custom_rules` with `path: '/dev/zero'`. `fileExists` passes, `stats.size` is 0, the guard passes, and `readFile` never reaches EOF. There is no `stats.isFile()` check, and the file can also grow between the stat and the read (TOCTOU).

`validate_custom_pattern` never checks flags, yet the CHANGELOG says both tools now enforce the flag allowlist. A pattern can be reported valid there and then fail, or compile differently, in `add_custom_rule`. `handleValidateCustomPattern` builds `customPattern` without a `flags` field, and `parseValidateCustomPatternInput` (inputParser.ts:416-427) does not parse `flags`. So the `ALLOWED_FLAGS_RE` branch in `validatePattern` can never fire for this tool. CHANGELOG.md says "user-supplied regex patterns in `add_custom_rule` and `validate_custom_pattern` are now validated for length (≤1 000 chars) and flag allowlist".

The flag strip/dedupe/default logic appears twice, so validation and execution can drift apart if one copy is edited. `pattern.flags.replace(/[^gimsuy]/g, '')`, `Array.from(new Set(stripped.split(''))).join('')` and the `'g'` fallback appear once in `executePattern` (lines 148-152) and again in `validatePattern` (lines 266-270). There is no shared helper.

The allowlist rejects valid JavaScript regex flags (`d`, `v`) that were accepted before, and at execution time silently strips them. That is a behaviour change the docs don't mention. `const ALLOWED_FLAGS_RE = /^[gimsuy]*$/;` makes `validatePattern` reject `flags: 'gd'` or `'v'`, which the old code (`new RegExp(pattern.pattern, pattern.flags || 'g')`) accepted. `executePattern` drops them with `replace(/[^gimsuy]/g, '')`.

The new handler tests don't show that the guard runs before the file is read, or that an accepted file is actually processed. They check only that an error was thrown or that a result exists. The oversize test asserts only `.rejects.toThrow(McpError)` and never asserts that the mocked `readFile` was not called, so 'before reading' is untested. The boundary test asserts only `.resolves.toBeDefined()`. Also, `setRequestHandler`'s capture condition `schema?.method === 'tools/call' || typeof handler === 'function'` matches every call, so the handler is really chosen by the 'last call' lookup in `beforeEach`.

The new length and flag limits leave ReDoS possible, allowing a custom rule to block the MCP server's event loop. add_custom_rule accepts '(a+)+$' with flag 'g' because it passes validatePattern; execute_custom_rules accepts 'a'.repeat(30) + '!' because it is below MAX_CODE_LENGTH. executePattern constructs a native RegExp and matchLineIssues calls regex.exec synchronously without a timeout or isolation. That exact regex/input exceeded a two-second subprocess timeout during review; larger inputs remain permitted. CHANGELOG.md claims these limits prevent ReDoS attacks.

With the default config the new activity test always passes, so check_staleness never increments the count and no market is ever skipped as stale; the staleness filter is effectively switched off. cli.py:299-315 runs check_staleness only on the output of filter_markets. scanner.py:71-73 drops any market where `vol = m.volume_24h if m.volume_24h > 0 else m.volume` is below sc.min_volume (config.py:536, default=100). staleness.py:72 computes the same `volume` and line 79 sets `has_volume = volume >= volume_floor` with volume_floor=10. Every candidate therefore has volume >= 100 >= 10, line 82 always takes the reset branch (`new_count = 0`), and line 97 `new_count >= threshold` is never true. Trigger: a market with a frozen price and frozen OI that passes filter_markets keeps count 0 on every scan and is never skipped.

Activity is measured from a rolling 24h volume (or, when that is 0, lifetime volume), not from trading since the previous cycle, so a market with no trades for many cycles still reads as active. Line 72 is `volume = m.volume_24h if m.volume_24h > 0 else m.volume`. Line 79 compares this absolute level to a floor and never to the stored `entry["volume"]`. A market that traded once within 24h, or that has any lifetime volume of 10 or more once volume_24h drops to 0 (`volume` is the API's total `volume` field, kalshi/markets.py:41), resets the count on every scan even though nothing traded between cycles. The volume delta that the old volume-spike logic tracked is gone.

Every test that expects a market to become stale uses volume=0, an input the production path never sends because filter_markets has already removed it, so the suite passes while the feature does nothing in real scans. test_inactive_market_increments_count, test_count_reaches_threshold_skips, test_no_volume_no_oi_no_price_increments and test_volume_below_floor_stale all build `_market(volume=0)` or `volume=9`. scanner.py:72 drops any candidate with volume below min_volume (default 100) before check_staleness runs. No test drives filter_markets and check_staleness together, or uses a realistic candidate (volume >= 100, unchanged price and OI) and expects it to be skipped.

The change edits the locked baseline acceptance tests so that they match the new implementation, which weakens their value as an independent gate. acceptance.md says 'The baseline's tests are the locked acceptance tests'. The diff rewrites existing tests in tests/unit/test_staleness.py: test_unchanged_price_increments_count becomes test_inactive_market_increments_count with volume changed from 500 to 0, test_volume_spike_resets_count is replaced, and the inputs of test_count_reaches_threshold_skips, test_price_change_resets_count and test_threshold_zero_disables change to volume=0. The packet contains no story.md that records who agreed the new expectations.

The activity floor of 10 is hard-coded, cannot be set from config, and is not tied to scanner.min_volume, which is how the floor and the volume filter came to conflict. `volume_floor: int = 10` is a keyword default. cli.py:312-315 calls check_staleness with only `threshold=staleness_threshold`. ScannerConfig has no matching field, and the new staleness_cycles description in config.py does not mention the floor.

StalenessEntry.volume is still written on every cycle but the new logic never reads it, which leaves dead state in the persisted file. Line 91 writes `volume=volume`, but lines 78-85 read only entry["price"], entry.get("open_interest", 0) and entry["count"]. The old read of entry["volume"] for the spike ratio was removed.

The new user-facing description promises that markets with active volume are not stale, but under the default min_volume no candidate can be stale at all, so the description misleads anyone tuning staleness_cycles. The description now reads 'Skip markets with no trading activity (no volume, no OI change, no price change)... Markets with stable prices but active volume are NOT considered stale.' Given scanner.py:72 and staleness.py:79, every candidate counts as having volume, so the setting has no effect.

Markets with zero recent trading can remain permanently exempt from staleness filtering because historical volume counts as current activity. Line 72 substitutes m.volume when volume_24h is zero, and has_volume now resets the count whenever that value exceeds 10. A market with volume=500, volume_24h=0, unchanged price and unchanged open interest therefore resets its count on every scan; seven repeated calls confirmed count=0 and no skips. filter_markets uses the same fallback, so this market also passes the default minimum-volume filter.

The change edits the locked acceptance tests so they skip the menu-action path the change rewired, so the tests no longer check that Pull and Push, as the user triggers them, finish and update the project. acceptance.md says "The baseline's tests are the locked acceptance tests". Yet the diff replaces `leftPlugin.pull!!.run()` / `push!!.run()` (the Runnable registered via addMenuAction) with `leftPlugin.plugin.pull()` / `push()`, and widens `pull`/`push` from `private` to `internal` in Plugin.kt (lines 540, 578) so they can be called. Under the new wiring (`addMenuAction("Pull") { kotlin.concurrent.thread { this.pull() } }`), the original `pull!!.run()` would return as soon as it started the thread, and the assertions would race the worker. The test was moved to match the implementation rather than the behaviour. No recorded reason or approver appears in the packet.

Nothing stops two Pull/Push operations from running at once, so a double key press, or a Push while a Pull's conflict dialog is open, runs two workers against the same repository files and loses or corrupts sync state. Each menu action and key binding (lines 44-54) starts a new `kotlin.concurrent.thread { this.pull() }` / `push()` with no lock, flag or single-thread executor. Before the change, `guiContext.uiRun(this::pull)` serialised them on the EDT. Each worker does readLocalRepository → projectToLocalRepository → readRemoteRepository → writeLocalRepository/writeRemoteRepository on the same `${options.repository}` and `.local` files (`File(...).writer()` truncates on open). For example: press ctrl+\ twice, or press ctrl+shift+\ while `dialogConflictResolver` blocks the first worker in `invokeAndWait`. The two threads interleave reads and writes, and one overwrites the other's merged version vectors, or one reads a half-written file and hits the "corrupt. Requires manual fixing" path.

The worker thread reads the project's renames and comments off the EDT and applies the merged result later through an asynchronous invokeLater, so any rename the user makes in between is silently overwritten and dropped from the local repository. `projectToLocalRepository` (called at lines 550 and 589) reads `context!!.args.codeData.renames/comments` on the background thread while the GUI can still change them. The merged state is written to disk (`writeLocalRepository`) and only afterwards applied in `uiRun { localRepositoryToProject(localRepository) ... }` (lines 572-575, 645-648). `localRepositoryToProject` calls `setProjectRenames(newProjectRenames)`, which replaces the whole list. A rename made while the pre-pull script runs, or while the conflict dialog is open, is therefore lost from the project and was never recorded in the `.local` file. Unsynchronised cross-thread access to the JadxCodeData lists is also a data race.

An unexpected exception in the new worker thread may end the Pull/Push silently, with no dialog, leaving the user unsure whether sync happened. `kotlin.concurrent.thread { this.pull() }` installs no try/catch and no uncaught-exception handler. Code reached from pull/push can throw: `context!!`, `localRepository!!`, `oldLocalRepositoryItem!!`, `newProjectItem!!`, `ProcessBuilder(command).start()` in `runScript` (throws IOException for a bad script path) and `process.waitFor()`. Before the change, these ran inside guiContext.uiRun on the EDT, where the host application's EDT exception handling applied. Now they go to the default thread handler, which only logs to stderr.

No test covers the threading the change introduces (background execution, EDT marshalling of the conflict dialog, async application of results), so a regression in any of it would pass the suite. The mock runs `uiRun` synchronously (`doAnswer { it.getArgument<Runnable>(0).run() }`). The tests call `plugin.pull()`/`push()` directly on the test thread, and each test passes its own conflictResolver lambda, so `dialogConflictResolver`'s `isEventDispatchThread`/`invokeAndWait` branches and the `InterruptedException`/`InvocationTargetException` handling are never run. Nothing exercises the `kotlin.concurrent.thread` wiring at lines 44-54 of Plugin.kt.

The new code uses fully-qualified names where the file and its neighbours use imports, and adds a second logger, which is inconsistent and harder to read. ConflictResolvers.kt already has `import javax.swing.*` yet writes `javax.swing.SwingUtilities.isEventDispatchThread()` and `javax.swing.SwingUtilities.invokeAndWait`. Plugin.kt writes `javax.swing.SwingUtilities.invokeLater` and `kotlin.concurrent.thread` inline. ConflictResolvers.kt adds a file-private `LOG = KotlinLogging.logger {}` even though `Plugin.LOG` (logger ID `jadx-collaboration`) exists, so conflict-dialog errors log under a different logger name than the rest of the plugin.

Renames and comments edited while a sync runs are silently overwritten when it completes. Start Pull with a slow pre-pull script, then edit a rename or comment in the responsive GUI. pull() captures project data in projectToLocalRepository() before running the script, then localRepositoryToProject() replaces the complete project rename and comment lists with that earlier snapshot plus remote changes. It never reconciles edits made during the script. push() has the same snapshot-and-replace sequence.

Repeated sync actions run concurrently against the same repository files, allowing stale results to overwrite newer changes. Every menu and keyboard invocation creates an independent thread without an in-flight guard or serialization. Trigger Pull while Push is waiting in its post-push script: both can read the same .local baseline, independently merge, and later overwrite .local and project state in completion order. writeRepository() also opens the shared destination directly with writer(), without locking or atomic replacement, so overlapping writes can corrupt the JSON.

The modified tests bypass the asynchronous entry points and leave the new threading behavior untested. RepositoryMockery now invokes plugin.pull() and plugin.push() directly instead of the registered menu callbacks. PluginMockery executes uiRun callbacks inline, and the diff adds no tests for worker execution, EDT dispatch, overlapping operations, or edits during synchronization; the existing assertions therefore cannot detect the concurrency regressions introduced here.

If the list query fails after Count succeeds, the handler returns 200 with an empty `entries` array plus a non-zero `total` and `has_more: true`. The UI then shows "No audit entries found" next to a Load more button, and the database error is never surfaced. Count errors are handled (`respondError(... "failed to count audit entries" ...)`), but `entries := a.reader.QuerySummaries(filter)` has no error return. `PGAuditReader.query` does `rows, err := r.pool.Query(...); if err != nil { return nil }`, and the handler turns nil into `[]types.AuditEntry{}`, then computes `"has_more": filter.Offset+len(entries) < total`.

While the detail fetch is loading, or after it fails, the expanded row shows the summary entry's blanked headers and bodies as if the request really had none. An admin reading the audit trail can conclude a request had an empty body. `const detailEntry = entryDetails[detailKey] ?? entry` falls back to the list entry. The server now blanks payloads for list entries (`'{}'::jsonb, ''::text, '{}'::jsonb, ''::text` in `auditSummarySelectCols`). The Request/Response Details blocks render `formatHeaders(detailEntry.request_headers)` and `formatBody(detailEntry.request_body, ...)` unconditionally, alongside the loading or error banner, instead of hiding them until `entryDetails[detailKey]` exists.

`total` and `entries` come from two separate queries that don't share a snapshot, so rows inserted between them can make `total`/`has_more` disagree with the page returned. `a.reader.Count(r.Context(), filter)` and `a.reader.QuerySummaries(filter)` each run their own pool query with no transaction. `query` also uses `context.Background()` rather than the request context, so a cancelled request doesn't stop the list query.

Every audit list request, including each Load more page and an unfiltered first page, now runs a `COUNT(*)` over `audit_log`. That is extra work on the hot path of a table that only grows. `Count` runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit_log al %s` with the same WHERE as the page query, and `handleAuditLog` calls it before every `QuerySummaries`. The value isn't cached and isn't skipped for later pages.

The new tests don't cover the pagination behaviour the change adds: the limit default and clamp, rejecting non-positive limits, `has_more` being true across pages, and stable ordering by `(timestamp, id)`. A wrong clamp or a wrong `has_more` formula would still pass. `TestAuditList_OmitsPayloadsAndReturnsTotal` inserts one entry, requests `limit=10`, and asserts only `total == 1` and `has_more == false`. No test sends `limit=0`, `limit=-1`, `limit=10000`, or an offset/limit that leaves more rows, and none asserts `limit` in the response equals `maxAuditLogLimit` (500).

The new `has_more` field is added to the client type but nothing uses it. The hook still derives `hasMore` from `entries.length < total`, which can drift because SSE `addEntry` changes both counts, so the server's flag is dead weight. `has_more?: boolean` is added to `AuditResponse`. `useAuditLog.ts:102` still returns `hasMore: entries.length < total`, and no file reads `has_more`.

The API docs aren't updated for the changed `GET /admin/audit` contract: list entries no longer include headers/bodies, `total` and `has_more` are new, and `limit` is capped at 500. API consumers have no record of the change. DESIGN.md:126 still reads `Query audit log (filters: decision, method, user, time range)` and web/README.md:181 reads `Query audit log with filters`. Neither mentions payload omission, the 500 cap, `total` or `has_more`, while the handler now applies `maxAuditLogLimit = 500` and serves `auditSummarySelectCols`.

Cached audit details never refresh, so reopening an entry can show an incomplete response even after the list reloads. toggleExpanded returns whenever entryDetails[detailKey] exists, and rendering always prefers that cached object over the current entry. If details are opened before a streamed response finishes, PGAuditReader.UpdateResponse subsequently updates the stored body, status and duration, but collapsing, changing filters and reopening the entry never fetches those updated details.

When a query has query_timeout/read timeout set and the timeout fires, the pg:query trace never completes: subscribers get a start event but no error, asyncStart or asyncEnd, so APM spans leak and the timeout error never reaches the tracer. Line 651 captures `queryCallback = query.callback` before tracing wraps it. Lines 726-735 then replace `query.callback` with the traced wrapper (around the timeout wrapper). On timeout the timer calls `queryCallback(error)` directly (line 660), which skips the traced wrapper, then sets `query.callback = () => {}` (line 664), dropping the traced wrapper so it is never called. No test covers this path.

Queries that fail straight away because the client is not queryable or is ending are never traced, so tracing tools never see these errors. The `!this._queryable` and `this._ending` branches (lines 689-701) return before the `shouldTrace(queryChannel)` block at line 709. They call `query.handleError` on the original, unwrapped callback.

Submittable queries with no callback (e.g. pg-cursor, pg-query-stream, or any `client.query(submittable)` used through events) are silently left out of the pg:query channel. The guard is `if (shouldTrace(queryChannel) && query.callback)`. A submittable passed without a callback has no `query.callback`, so it goes to `enqueue()` with no trace.

For multi-statement simple queries, `context.result.rowCount` and `command` are undefined, because the callback receives an array of Results rather than one Result. query.js line 142 calls `this.callback(null, this._results)`, and `_results` can be an array for multi-statement text. enrichedCb reads `res.rowCount` / `res.command` without checking for an array.

On Node versions where TracingChannel lacks the `hasSubscribers` getter (Node 18), every query, client connect and pool connect goes through traceCallback even with no subscribers. That is extra closures and wrapping on the hot path, and it is the same configuration the new tests skip as unstable. `shouldTrace` returns `channel.hasSubscribers !== false`, which is true when the getter is undefined. Both test files set `hasStableTracingChannel` to require a boolean `hasSubscribers` and skip otherwise, with the comment 'Skip tests on older versions where TracingChannel is missing or has internal bugs'. So the always-on production path on those versions is never exercised. pg's engines field is `>= 16.0.0`.

The full SQL text goes out to any diagnostics_channel subscriber. If an app builds SQL with inlined literals, those values (possibly sensitive) are exposed to every in-process subscriber, and nothing documents this. `context = { query: { text: query.text, ... } }` is published on start. No redaction option exists and no documentation mentions the channel payloads.

The native client (pg.native) gets no instrumentation, so the pg:query and pg:connection channels stay silent for users of pg-native. The diff only changes packages/pg/lib/client.js. packages/pg/lib/native/client.js has its own connect/query methods and does not use `./diagnostics`.

The diagnostics loader and `shouldTrace` are copied into two packages, and the connection-context literal is duplicated within Client.connect, so future fixes have to be made in several places. packages/pg-pool/diagnostics.js and packages/pg/lib/diagnostics.js contain the same try/getBuiltInModule block and the same `shouldTrace` function. client.js lines 329 and 350 build the identical `connection: { database, host, port, user, ssl }` object twice.

The new public channels (pg:query, pg:connection, pg:pool:connect, pg:pool:release, pg:pool:remove) and their payload shapes are undocumented, so integrators have to reverse-engineer them from the code. A search of the repo for 'diagnostics_channel' or 'pg:query' finds only the two new diagnostics.js modules and their tests. No README or docs page changed.

The new tests cover only the happy path and one error per channel, and leave out the paths most likely to break, such as query timeouts, non-queryable clients, the pool's connectionTimeoutMillis queue path and connect errors. The query tests cover callback success, an errorMessage, client info and the promise path. The pool tests cover one successful connect (via a mock client), release and remove. None set `query_timeout` or `connectionTimeoutMillis`, and none fail a connect, which is how the read-timeout trace leak goes undetected.

The tracing callbacks expose raw clients and query rows through diagnostic contexts despite constructing limited metadata objects. TracingChannel.traceCallback assigns the callback's second argument to context.result before publishing asyncStart. For pool.connect(), that argument is the full Client, and enrichedCb never replaces context.result; a Node 22 reproduction confirmed asyncEnd receives the Client instance. Client contains connectionParameters and password. The same pattern in packages/pg/lib/client.js:726 exposes the full query Result, including rows, to asyncStart before enrichedCb replaces it with command and rowCount.

Queries that reach their read timeout never publish tracing completion or error events, leaving subscribers with unfinished operations. The readTimeout handler captures queryCallback before tracing is installed, calls queryCallback(error) directly, and replaces query.callback with a no-op. The new traceCallback wrapper is installed only afterward at line 728. When a queued or active query times out, the timeout therefore bypasses that wrapper, and the scheduled query.handleError also reaches the replacement no-op; subscribers receive start/end but neither error nor asyncEnd.

Enabling query tracing changes the callback receiver, which can break callbacks that access the Query through this. Query.handleReadyForQuery and Query.handleError invoke callbacks as this.callback(...), preserving the Query receiver. The tracing wrapper receives that receiver, but enrichedCb is an arrow function and invokes origCb(err, res) as a plain function, discarding it. Thus the same callback receives the Query without tracing and undefined as this in strict mode when tracing is subscribed.

S3 sync can never work: the adapter calls a getPresignedUrl IPC that nothing implements, and it reads config keys the UI never writes. getPresignedUrl checks `api?.getPresignedUrl` and throws if it is missing, but electron/preload.js exposes no getPresignedUrl and electron/main.js registers no 'get-presigned-url' handler (a grep for presigned across the repo only finds docs and this file). The adapter also passes `keyId: config.keyId, secret: config.secret`, while the SyncTab S3 fields are named `accessKeyId` and `secretAccessKey`. Every S3 Push/Pull throws 'requires Electron', even inside Electron. README and WORKSPACES.md document S3 as working.

Sync credentials (AWS secret key, git PAT, bearer and JWT tokens) are written to disk and to localStorage in plaintext, although the docs and types say they are encrypted. writeSyncConfig stores `{ provider, config }` as-is in sync-config.json and also mirrors it with `lsWrite(LS_SYNC_CONFIG, ...)` even in Electron. encryptValue/decryptValue are defined but never called anywhere (grep finds only their definitions). WORKSPACES.md says 'Sensitive sync credentials ... are encrypted using Electron's safeStorage API before being written to sync-config.json'.

The new git routes accept a filesystem root from any caller and run git there, and the server has no authentication, CORS allows every origin, and it listens on all interfaces, so a web page or LAN host can create repos, write files and run git push/pull to an attacker-chosen remote anywhere on the user's disk. `const dataDir = req.body.dataDir || process.env.APILIX_DATA_DIR;` comes from the request body. ensureRepo then runs mkdirSync, git init, addRemote(config.remote) and addConfig under `path.join(dataDir,'git-sync','workspaces')`. The server uses `app.use(cors())` and `app.listen(PORT)` with no host. The workspaceId guard `repoDir.startsWith(path.resolve(repoBase))` lacks a path separator, so a workspaceId of `../workspaces-x` also passes. main.js already sets APILIX_DATA_DIR, so the body value isn't needed.

The git token gets saved in plaintext in the local repo's .git/config, which contradicts the docs' claim that the credential URL is never stored. The push route builds `url.username/url.password` into `remote`, then calls `git.push(remote, branch, ['--set-upstream'])`. With a URL as the remote, --set-upstream writes `branch.<branch>.remote = https://user:token@host/...` into the repo config under userData/git-sync. WORKSPACES.md says 'the credential-embedded URL is never stored'.

Conflict detection never fires, so Pull silently overwrites local changes. lastSynced is never recorded, and the comparison is a string compare across mismatched date formats. pull only throws ConflictError when `remoteTs && localTs && remoteTs > localTs`, with `localTs = syncConfig.lastSynced ?? null`. No code sets lastSynced: SyncTab builds `{ workspaceId, provider, config: fields }` and writeSyncConfig stores only provider and config. Even if it were set, `>` compares an RFC 1123 `Last-Modified` string ('Mon, 01 ...') with an ISO string lexicographically. Both README and WORKSPACES.md promise a conflict banner.

If a git push fails after the commit is made (network or auth error), every later Push reports success without pushing that commit. The push route runs `git.add('.')` and `git.commit(...)` before `git.push(...)`. On retry, `status.files.length === 0` returns `{ ok: true, message: 'Nothing to commit' }` before it reaches push, so the client shows 'Pushed successfully' while the remote stays behind.

Choosing 'Keep Local' on the conflict banner shows the misleading message 'Remote is empty — nothing to pull'. The Keep Local button calls `handlePull('keep-local')`. syncEngine.pull returns null for keep-local ('caller will push instead'), and handlePull treats null as `setMsg('Remote is empty — nothing to pull')`. No push follows.

Snapshot files are never deleted, so disk use grows without limit: a full copy of the workspace is written about 300 ms after each change. The docs say the oldest snapshot is deleted. createSnapshot writes `snapshots/{id}.json` and then only trims the index with `[entry, ...idx].slice(0, MAX_SNAPSHOTS)`. Pruned snapshot files are never removed. store.tsx calls createSnapshot from a 300 ms debounce (`setTimeout(..., 300)`) on every collection or environment change. WORKSPACES.md says snapshots are taken about 1–2 s after the last change and that 'the oldest snapshot is automatically deleted'.

The rewrite drops restore of open request tabs, so tabs that used to survive a restart are now lost. The old useReducer initializer rebuilt `tabs`/`activeTabId` from `saved.tabSession`, and the old persistence effect wrote tabSession. The new code (`useReducer(appReducer, initialState)` plus a WorkspaceData-only write) never saves or restores tabs, and the PersistedState.tabSession type is now unused.

If storage init throws (an IPC error, a corrupt JSON file, or a failed write), the app hangs on the 'Loading…' screen with no error or recovery. `init()` is called without try/catch or .catch. The read-json-file IPC rethrows parse errors other than ENOENT, and writeManifest/writeWorkspace don't catch IPC errors. HYDRATE_WORKSPACE then never dispatches, so storageReady stays false, and AppProvider renders only 'Loading…' while storageReady is false.

Deleting a workspace leaves its snapshot history (full copies of its data) on disk. handleDelete calls StorageDriver.deleteWorkspace, which removes only `workspaces/{id}.json` and the localStorage key. The `workspaces/{id}/history.json` and `snapshots/` directory that snapshotEngine writes are left behind, although the UI says 'This cannot be undone'.

The lockfile lists bcryptjs and jsonwebtoken as root dependencies that server/package.json doesn't declare, so the two are out of sync, and nothing in the repo uses these packages. The lock's root `dependencies` gains `"bcryptjs": "^3.0.3"` and `"jsonwebtoken": "^9.0.3"`, but server/package.json adds only simple-git. `npm ci` refuses to install when package.json and the lockfile disagree. The team server that would use them isn't in the repo.

The change adds the simple-git dependency with no recorded vetting, and the code treats it as optional, which hides an install failure until runtime. `"simple-git": "^3.35.2"` is added. server/index.js wraps `require('simple-git')` in try/catch and returns 501 if it is missing. The packet's risk.json requires gate:deps for this dependency.

Dead code: ActivityBar adds a manageOpen state and a WorkspaceManagerModal, but nothing ever opens it. `const [manageOpen, setManageOpen] = useState(false)` is never set to true in ActivityBar. Only the `onClose` path calls setManageOpen.

The Team tab never creates or marks a team workspace, so the switcher's 'Team' group and the role badges can't appear, and the docs describe a team-server flow the app doesn't support. TeamTab only does a test fetch of `${serverUrl}/workspaces`. `dispatch` is destructured but unused. No code sets `type: 'team'`, `role` or `teamServerUrl`. teamAdapter's header refers to `server/team/`, which doesn't exist in the repo.

emptyWorkspaceData and PRESET_COLORS are copied across three files (the switcher, the modal and store.tsx's inline defaults), so they can drift apart. The same `emptyWorkspaceData()` body appears in both WorkspaceSwitcher.tsx and WorkspaceManagerModal.tsx, and store.tsx init repeats the same literal. The PRESET_COLORS array is declared in both components.

The diff includes unrelated changes the workspace story doesn't explain: a websocket-toggle light-mode colour and a RequestBuilder tab-cache change. index.css adds `html.light .bg-purple-700` with the comment 'Keep selected websocket toggle readable'. RequestBuilder.tsx changes `cacheRef.current.set(..., { edit, dirty: false, activeRequestTab })` in two places. Neither relates to workspaces.

The change adds persistence migration, sync engines, git server routes and IPC file handlers with no tests, so the defects above were never exercised. No test files exist in the repo (a glob for **/*.test.* finds none), and the diff adds none for storageDriver, syncEngine, snapshotEngine, the reducer's workspace actions or /api/sync/git/*.

Unauthenticated Git sync requests can write repositories outside the application's trusted data directory. The server enables unrestricted cors() and listens without a host restriction or authentication middleware. POST /api/sync/git/push accepts dataDir from the request, constructs its containment boundary from that same untrusted value, then calls ensureRepo(), writes workspace.json, stages files and pushes to a caller-supplied remote. The startsWith check also accepts sibling paths such as workspaceId '../workspaces-other'.

Saving sync configuration persists access tokens and AWS secrets in plaintext on disk and in localStorage. SyncTab.saveConfig passes the input fields directly to writeSyncConfig. That function assigns the unchanged config to store, writes it to sync-config.json and mirrors it with lsWrite. The encryptValue and decryptValue helpers have no callers, so Electron safeStorage does not protect saved credentials.

S3 push and pull always fail, including inside Electron. Both operations call getPresignedUrl(), which throws when electronAPI.getPresignedUrl is absent. electron/preload.js never exposes that method, and electron/main.js contains no presigning handler. Additionally, the adapter reads keyId and secret while the UI supplies accessKeyId and secretAccessKey.

Switching or creating a workspace shortly after an edit silently loses the outgoing workspace's changes. The persistence effect schedules the current workspace write after 300 ms and clears that timer on cleanup. WorkspaceSwitcher.handleSwitch reads only the destination and dispatches SWITCH_WORKSPACE without saving the outgoing state; handleCreate likewise dispatches CREATE_WORKSPACE. Either action changes activeWorkspaceId and cancels the pending outgoing write before replacing its collections and variables.

Pulling remote data bypasses conflict detection and overwrites local changes without offering resolution. handlePull constructs SyncConfig with only workspaceId, provider and config. syncEngine.pull requires both remoteTs and syncConfig.lastSynced before throwing ConflictError. No caller supplies lastSynced and no successful sync persists it, so the conflict branch is unreachable from the UI and returned remote data is immediately hydrated and written over the workspace.

Retrying a failed Git push reports success without uploading the pending commit. The route commits before calling git.push. If that push fails, the commit remains locally. Retrying with unchanged workspace data produces status.files.length === 0 and returns 'Nothing to commit' before git.push executes, even when the network or credentials have been corrected.

Saving sync settings for another workspace in browser mode erases previously saved workspace configurations. writeSyncConfig initializes store to {} and reads existing configuration only inside if (api). Without Electron, it never reads LS_SYNC_CONFIG before lsWrite replaces the entire key with the current workspace entry. Saving workspace B therefore removes workspace A's configuration.

Snapshot retention trims only the index, leaving full snapshot files to accumulate indefinitely. createSnapshot writes a new snapshot on every debounced save, slices the history index to MAX_SNAPSHOTS and writes that index. It never deletes the snapshot files whose entries were removed, despite WORKSPACES.md stating that the oldest snapshot is automatically deleted at the 50-snapshot limit.

If a checkpoint file exists but fails to load, the pipeline skips training. It then reports p-values from an untrained, freshly initialised model and never overwrites the bad checkpoint. `load_model` catches every exception and returns `(None, None)`. The `model is None` branch then sets `q` from `find_latent_dim` and builds a new model with `init_model`. `model_was_loaded = (checkpoint_path and checkpoint_path.exists() and q is not None)` only checks that the file exists and that `q` is set, so it is True, `should_train` is False and `save_model` is never reached. Trigger: run once with the default out_dir (model.pt is saved), then rerun with input whose protein count differs after filtering. `load_state_dict` raises a size mismatch, the error is swallowed, and results come from the untrained model. A second trigger is `init_pca=False`: the saved encoder has no bias, but `load_model` builds with `prot_means=None`, so the encoder has a bias, the strict load fails, and the same path runs on every rerun.

`protrider plot encoding_dim` now fails after a grid-search run. The change no longer writes the file the plot reads and renamed its columns. The diff removes `df_gs.to_csv(f'{out_dir}/grid_search.csv')` from `find_latent_dim`. The new `GridSearchResult.to_csv` writes `grid_search_results.csv` with columns `enc_dim`/`auprc`. `plot_encoding_dim` still runs `pd.read_csv(output_dir + "/grid_search.csv")` and uses the `encod_dim`/`aucpr` columns, so it raises FileNotFoundError on new output.

Removing the cross-validation fields breaks every existing user config that still has `cross_val`. The repo's previous `config.yaml` template shipped `cross_val: False`. The diff deletes `cross_val`, `n_folds`, `early_stopping_patience`, `early_stopping_min_delta` and `fit_every_fold` from `ProtriderConfig`. `load_config` calls `ProtriderConfig(**config_dict)` and turns the TypeError into `ValueError("Invalid configuration ...")`, so `protrider run --config old.yaml` fails at startup. The whole CV mode (cv.py, `train_val`, `plot_cv_loss`, `_run_protrider_cv`) is removed with no deprecation path.

The change deletes and edits locked baseline acceptance tests so the build passes, instead of keeping them as the judge. acceptance.md says the baseline's tests are the locked acceptance tests. The diff deletes all of tests/test_pipeline_cv.py (k-fold, LOOCV, early stopping, fit_every_fold), removes the `cross_val`/`n_folds`/... arguments from tests/test_config.py, and rewrites the unpacking of `run()` in test_pipeline_features/misc/standard to `result, *_ = run(config)`. Nothing else now checks the removed CV behaviour.

In grid or binary search, a candidate q whose training loss is non-finite crashes the search instead of being skipped. In `train_and_eval_q`, the `if ~np.isfinite(loss):` branch assigns `auc_prec_rec = np.nan`, but the function returns `auprc`, which is only assigned in the else branch. The result is UnboundLocalError. The old loop simply did not append that q.

The new 'bs' (binary search) logic is wrong. After the shrink step it always runs a shift step too, it never uses the computed upper bound, and it can miss the best evaluated q. The `if fM >= fL and fM >= fR:` shrink block is followed by an unconditional `if fR > fM: ... else: ...` rather than `elif`, so each iteration both shrinks and shifts. `k_max = injected_dataset.X.shape[1]` and `tol` are computed but never used, and `R = int(q * 3)` can exceed the number of samples or proteins. `best_q` is updated only at the top of each iteration, so points evaluated in the last iteration are recorded in `enc2auprc` but never compared. The loop variable `q` also shadows the outer `q`.

With `common_degrees_freedom=False`, the fallback degrees of freedom depends on protein order. Non-converged proteins also get a df that does not match their fitted mu and sigma. Inside `for j, _mu, _sigma, _df in results:`, `df0` is recomputed from `np.nanmedian(df)` over the entries filled so far. The first 10 proteins always fall back to 10, later ones get a running median, and this costs O(n²) work. When the first-pass df exceeded `max_df` (set to NaN), `mu[j]`/`sigma[j]` keep the jointly fitted values from the huge df, but `df[j]` is set to `df0` without refitting.

A checkpoint is loaded with `torch.load(..., weights_only=False)` from `out_dir/model.pt` automatically. This may let a crafted or swapped .pt file run arbitrary code through pickle. In `load_model`, the call is `checkpoint = torch.load(checkpoint_path, map_location=config.device_torch, weights_only=False)`. The checkpoint only holds a state_dict plus ints and bools, which `weights_only=True` can load. `run()` calls it whenever `<out_dir>/model.pt` exists, without the user opting in.

A previous run's model is silently reused even when the input data or model config has changed, as long as the tensor shapes match. Results can come from a model trained on different data or settings. Checkpointing is on by default (`checkpoint_path = Path(config.out_dir) / 'model.pt'`). The checkpoint stores only `q`, `n_layers` and `presence_absence`. `find_q_method`, `lr`, `n_epochs`, `cov_used`, `init_pca` and the input file are not compared, and `h_dim` is taken from the current config. Training is skipped whenever loading succeeds, so rerunning with new samples or settings into the same out_dir reuses the stale model.

Unrequested behaviour changes alter results for every run: early stopping on training loss with weight restore, an LR scheduler, and a changed multi-layer architecture (bias added, GELU instead of ReLU). `train()` now adds `ReduceLROnPlateau(... patience=patience // 4)` and early stopping on `running_loss` that restores `best_model_wts`. It still returns the last epoch's `running_loss`, not the restored model's loss. `ConditionalEnDecoder` changes `nn.Linear(in_dim, h_dim, bias=False)` + `nn.ReLU()` to `nn.Linear(in_dim, h_dim)` + `nn.GELU()`. Separately, the df floor `df0 = max(df0, 3.0)` is added to the common-df path.

A new dependency (wandb, with its transitive stack) is added and the lockfile regenerated, and nothing in the change shows it was vetted. pyproject adds `[project.optional-dependencies] wandb = ["wandb"]`, unpinned. uv.lock adds wandb 0.24.0 plus sentry-sdk, gitpython, protobuf, pydantic, requests, urllib3 and others, and rewrites resolution markers to split on sys_platform. risk.json flags this dependency class as unplanned.

The default for `common_degrees_freedom` differs between the Python API and the shipped config template, so CLI and API users get different p-value models by default. config.py sets `common_degrees_freedom: bool = True`, but config.yaml sets `common_degrees_freedom: False`. Both carry the comment 'more stable for small datasets'. The README does not document the parameter.

The end-to-end checkpoint tests cannot detect whether the model was actually loaded, or whether training was wrongly skipped. `test_default_checkpoint_behavior` and `test_custom_checkpoint_path` use `find_q_method='5'` and assert only `model_info1.q == model_info2.q`. That holds whether or not the second run loaded the checkpoint. No test covers a checkpoint that exists but fails to load, which is the path in the model_was_loaded finding.

`find_latent_dim` always runs SVD and OHT, even for a fixed integer q, and for non-search methods it returns an empty GridSearchResult instead of None. The CLI then writes an empty grid_search_results.csv. `dataset.perform_svd(); q = dataset.find_enc_dim_optht()` runs unconditionally at the top (and again in the 'gs' branch). `gs_result = GridSearchResult(enc_dim=np.array(list(enc2auprc.keys())), ...)` is always built, so the cli.py guard `if gs_results is not None: gs_results.to_csv(...)` always fires.

A leftover debug `print` writes to stdout during grid search. `_get_gs_params` begins with `print(data_shape)`. Also, `a = max(a, oht_q//2)` can exceed `b`, which yields a descending or degenerate grid.

Parquet reading is forced to the fastparquet engine, an unexplained change from pandas' default (pyarrow), which is also a dependency. `pd.read_parquet(input_intensities)` became `pd.read_parquet(input_intensities, engine='fastparquet')`.

A failed checkpoint load causes training to be skipped and results to be computed from a newly initialized model. If an existing checkpoint is corrupt or has incompatible tensor shapes, load_model catches the error and returns (None, None). run then initializes a fresh model and assigns q, so checkpoint_path.exists() and q is not None become true at line 509. should_train is false despite loading having failed.

The new grid-search output format breaks the encoding-dimension plotting command. GridSearchResult.to_csv writes grid_search_results.csv with enc_dim and auprc columns, and cli.run uses this writer. plots.plot_encoding_dim still reads grid_search.csv and accesses encod_dim and aucpr. After a fresh grid-search run, the documented encoding_dim plot fails because its expected file is absent.

Checkpoint reuse can silently apply weights to different proteins or covariates and produce incorrect outlier results. Run once, then reorder protein rows in the input while retaining the same proteins and output directory. run automatically loads model.pt; save_model stores weights and architecture metadata but no protein or covariate identifiers. load_model checks tensor compatibility only, so the reordered dataset has matching shapes and loads successfully, while weight positions now refer to different proteins. Training is then skipped.

Models trained with init_pca=False cannot be restored faithfully from their checkpoints. init_model passes dataset.prot_means_torch when init_wPCA is false. ConditionalEnDecoder consequently subtracts these means and creates an encoder without bias. save_model does not preserve prot_means, while load_model always constructs with prot_means=None, creating an encoder bias and removing centering. load_state_dict therefore rejects the missing bias key for these saved models.

A nonfinite training loss crashes latent-dimension search instead of returning an unsuccessful candidate score. In train_and_eval_q, a NaN or infinite loss enters the branch assigning auc_prec_rec = np.nan, but the function returns auprc at line 86. auprc is assigned only in the finite-loss branch, so this path raises UnboundLocalError for both grid and binary search.

The freshness check runs after MinimizeCopilotComments, so when the latest Copilot review is up to date the tool still hides it as OUTDATED and then exits without asking for a new one. The user ends up with no visible current review. In run(), client.MinimizeCopilotComments(prNumber) at line 47 runs first and minimizes every non-minimized Copilot review with classifier OUTDATED. Only then does IsCopilotReviewFresh run (line 73), and if it is true the function prints "Copilot review is already up to date" and returns. Trigger: a PR whose last Copilot review was submitted after the last commit. The fresh review is minimized as outdated and no re-review is requested.

The commits and reviews lists are not paginated, so on a PR with more than 30 commits (the GitHub REST default page size) lastCommitDate comes from commit 30, not the newest commit. A stale Copilot review can then count as fresh and the re-review is wrongly skipped. c.rest.Get(fmt.Sprintf("repos/%s/%s/pulls/%d/commits", ...), &commits) is called once with no per_page or page loop, and lastCommitDate := commits[len(commits)-1].Commit.Committer.Date takes the last item of that single page. The reviews call at line 100 has the same problem, so the latest Copilot review can also be missed.

Freshness compares the commit's committer date, which is set on the client, with the review's submitted time. Commits made locally before a review but pushed after it look older than the review. The tool then reports the review as up to date and skips a review the new code needs. lastCommitDate := commits[len(commits)-1].Commit.Committer.Date, then return latestCopilotReview.After(lastCommitDate). Committer date is git metadata, not push time, so clock skew or a delayed push breaks the comparison. The code never compares the review's commit_id with the PR head SHA, which would avoid this.

Any submitted Copilot review counts toward freshness, including DISMISSED ones, so a dismissed review can stop a new request. The loop only checks isCopilotUser(r.User.Login) && r.SubmittedAt.After(latestCopilotReview). It never reads the review state, unlike HasCopilotPendingReview, which filters on State.

The new branching behaviour comes with no tests: the repository has no _test.go files and the diff adds none, so fresh, stale, no-review and many-commit cases are all unchecked. The export contains only cmd/root.go, internal/github/github.go, main.go and version/version.go as Go sources. The diff adds IsCopilotReviewFresh and an early return in run() but no test file.

The README is now out of date: it does not mention the new skip when the Copilot review is newer than the last commit, and its step order (check status, then hide old reviews) does not match what the code does. README lines 7 and 26 list only 'already requested or in progress' as reasons to exit early. The diff adds a third early exit with the message "Copilot review is already up to date (newer than the last commit)", and the README was not changed.

Each run fetches the same reviews endpoint twice, once in HasCopilotPendingReview and again in IsCopilotReviewFresh, which costs an extra API call and repeats the same struct and loop logic. Both functions call c.rest.Get(fmt.Sprintf("repos/%s/%s/pulls/%d/reviews", ...)) and loop over the reviews filtering with isCopilotUser. run() calls them one after the other at lines 64 and 73.

An up-to-date Copilot review is hidden before the command skips requesting a replacement. For a PR with an unminimized Copilot review submitted after its last commit, run first calls MinimizeCopilotComments, which minimizes every unminimized Copilot review as OUTDATED. The new freshness check then returns true and exits without requesting another review, leaving the current review hidden.

The freshness check reads only the first page of commits and reviews, causing incorrect decisions on longer PRs. IsCopilotReviewFresh makes one Get call per endpoint without pagination and treats commits[len(commits)-1] as the latest commit. Both endpoints paginate with a default of 30 results. With 31 commits and a Copilot review between commits 30 and 31, it can report fresh and suppress the needed request; a fresh review beyond the first 30 reviews can instead be missed. See [GitHub pull request documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/pulls#list-commits-on-a-pull-request) and [review documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/reviews#list-reviews-for-a-pull-request).

After a basemap switch the other layers are never remounted, because the code calls each layer atom as a plain function (`layer('disable')`) instead of dispatching its actions. Every overlay disappears from the map when the style changes. `mountedLayersAtom` holds `LayerAtom` values, typed `AtomSelfBinded<LogicalLayerState, LogicalLayerActions>` in types/logicalLayer.ts:40. In `logicalLayerFabric.ts`, enable and disable only take effect through dispatched actions (`onAction('disable', ...)` pushes `enabledLayersAtom.delete(id)`). The repo's working pattern is `store.dispatch([layerAtom.disable(), ...]); store.dispatch([layerAtom.enable()])` in applyNewLayerSource.ts:10-19. Trigger: a user enables a `maplibre-style-url` layer while another layer is mounted. `map.setStyle(styleUrl)` drops the custom layers, and the `styledata` callback then runs `layer('disable'); layer('enable')`, which calls the atom's reducer with a string and dispatches nothing. `enabledLayersAtom` and `mountedLayersAtom` stay the same, so `willMount` never runs again. Even with real dispatches, a disable and an enable in the same synchronous run would need separate dispatches, as applyNewLayerSource does.

The test passes against the broken remount path. It stands in a `vi.fn()` for the layer atom and only checks that the function was called with 'disable', not that any layer was actually unmounted and mounted again. `const otherLayer = vi.fn(); mountedLayersAtom.set.dispatch('other', otherLayer as any)`, then `otherLayer.mock.calls.filter((call) => call[0] === 'disable').length > 0`. A real `LayerAtom` is never called this way, and the test never asserts that 'enable' was called. It checks the order of calls on a fake (L3.20), not the state of `enabledLayersAtom`/`mountedLayersAtom` or that the renderer's `willMount` ran. `once` is mocked to fire `styledata` synchronously, and `layersOrderManager.init` is replaced with a no-op without checking that it was called.

`setStyle` runs on every `_updateMap` call: the first mount, and every later legend or source update of the basemap layer. Each run reloads the whole basemap and tries to remount every other layer, even when the style URL hasn't changed. `willMount`, `willLegendUpdate` and `willSourceUpdate` all call `_updateMap`, which runs `map.setStyle(styleUrl)` with no check against the current style. boot.ts:107-134 (`getBaseMapUrl`) already sets the enabled basemap's URL as `mapBaseStyle`. So when the default basemap layer mounts on page load, the same style is applied a second time and all custom layers go through the remove/remount path.

PKCE is optional: a client that omits code_challenge gets a code that /token swaps for the user's GitHub token with no verifier and no client authentication, even though Discovery advertises S256 and MCP/OAuth 2.1 public clients are expected to use PKCE. Authorize only checks the method `if codeChallenge != "" && codeChallengeMethod != "S256"`, so an empty challenge passes. ExchangeCode in session.go skips verification with `if sess.CodeChallenge != "" { verifyPKCE(...) }`. Token never checks client_id or a client secret. Anyone holding the internal code and redirect_uri gets the GitHub access_token back.

The client-supplied `state` is used as the server-side session key and silently overwritten, so a second /authorize call with the same state replaces another flow's redirect_uri and code_challenge before its GitHub callback lands (session fixation or hijack of an in-flight flow). SaveSession does `s.sessions[state] = &Session{...}` with no check for an existing entry. Callback then looks up only by `state` (HasSession and CompleteCallback) and redirects to whatever `sess.RedirectURI` the most recent /authorize stored. Nothing binds the browser that started /authorize to the one that hits /callback (no cookie or server-generated nonce).

Replaying /callback for one state mints several internal codes for the same session. Exchanging one deletes only that code, so the others can still be exchanged for the access token until the session expires, which defeats one-time use. CompleteCallback assigns a new `code` and `s.codes[code] = sess` on every call, without removing an earlier sess.InternalCode. ExchangeCode does `delete(s.codes, code); delete(s.sessions, sess.State)`, but any other entries in s.codes still point to the same *Session, whose ExpiresAt is unchanged and whose AccessToken is still set.

Unauthenticated /authorize creates a session for every distinct state value, with no cap or rate limit, so a local caller can grow the session map without bound for the 10-minute TTL and run the 256M container out of memory. Authorize sits on the public mux (`mux.HandleFunc("GET /authorize", ...)` in main.go). Each valid request calls `h.store.SaveSession(state, ...)` into an unbounded map, and the janitor only clears entries after ExpiresAt. The port is bound to 127.0.0.1, which limits who can reach it but does not bound the map.

When the user denies consent or GitHub returns an error, the façade answers with a bare 400 instead of redirecting `error=` back to the MCP client's redirect_uri, so the client's login flow hangs and the session is left behind. Callback reads only `code` and `state` and returns `http.Error(w, "missing code or state", http.StatusBadRequest)` when code is empty. GitHub's `error`/`error_description` query parameters are never read or forwarded to sess.RedirectURI.

The new authentication, session and PKCE code ships with no tests, and CI has no Go job, so none of the security behaviour (redirect allowlist, PKCE, one-time codes, expiry, 401 vs 503) is checked on any build. The diff adds handler.go, session.go and middleware/auth.go but no *_test.go files. .github/workflows/lint-test.yml runs only `npm test`, shellcheck and bats, with no `go test` or `go vet`.

The default OAuth scope `repo,user` asks for full read/write on all private repositories and write access to the user's profile, more than a PR-review service needs, and the token is handed straight to the MCP client. `GITHUB_OAUTH_SCOPES=${GITHUB_OAUTH_SCOPES:-repo,user}` here and the matching default in main.go loadConfig. ValidateToken only needs `/user` (read:user would do), and Token returns the raw GitHub `access_token` to the caller.

The validated-token cache keeps accepting a GitHub token for up to TOKEN_CACHE_TTL_MIN after it is revoked, and the middleware accepts any valid GitHub token (any app or PAT, any user), not just tokens this façade issued. ValidateToken returns early on `h.store.LookupToken(token)` without contacting GitHub. middleware.Auth accepts any token for which ValidateToken returns a login, and there is no user allowlist or token-origin check.

The Token doc comment says the client_id is validated by GitHub during the code exchange, but /token never reads client_id. GitHub only ever sees the façade's own client_id, so the comment misstates the security model. Token reads only grant_type, code, redirect_uri and code_verifier. exchangeGitHubCode sends `h.cfg.GitHubClientID` from config, not anything the MCP client presented.

SESSION_TTL_MIN and TOKEN_CACHE_TTL_MIN accept 0 or negative values with no validation.
