A truncated or malformed JFIF APP0 segment makes FastImage.resolution raise NoMethodError to the caller even with raise_on_failure false, where every other parse failure returns nil. `data = @stream.read(length)` uses the segment's declared length. Once `data[0, 5] == "JFIF\0"` matches, `data[7].ord` and `data[8, 4].unpack("nn")` run with no length check. A declared length of 7 to 11 bytes makes `data[7]` or the slice nil, so the call raises NoMethodError. `fetch` (fastimage.rb:293-298) only rescues the listed fetch/parse errors (CannotParseImage, EOFError, etc.), so NoMethodError reaches the user. A length field under 2 makes `read(-n)` return nil, and `data[0,5]` raises the same way.

For JPEGs with a JFIF APP0 segment, the JFIF density is returned straight away and any EXIF XResolution/YResolution is ignored. A file written with the common JFIF placeholder (units 0, density 1:1) and a real EXIF DPI may therefore report [[1,1], :no_units] instead of its actual resolution. In the `MARKER_APP0` branch, `return [[x_density, y_density], unit_sym]` runs for any JFIF segment, including `JFIF_UNIT_ASPECT_RATIO` (mapped to :no_units). APP0 normally comes before APP1, so `exif_resolution` is never consulted. The locked fixture expects `"test3.jpg"=>[..., [[1, 1], :no_units]]`, so this precedence is never tested against a file that has both.

TIFF/EXIF XResolution and YResolution values stored before the IFD are silently dropped. TIFFs that keep IFD0 at the end of the file (a common writer layout) may therefore return nil resolution even though they have one. `read_rational_resolution` computes `skip_amount = absolute_pos - @stream.pos` and does `next if skip_amount < 0`. The stream only moves forward, so any rational offset before the current position is skipped without a value. Nothing records or reports this, and no fixture covers that layout ("test.dng" is expected to be nil without explanation).

When an image has no resolution, `@resolution` is never assigned. Each later call to `resolution` or `resolution_units` on the same instance re-fetches the image, which for a URL means a new HTTP request. `parse_resolution` returning nil makes `parse_packets` raise CannotParseImage, which `fetch` swallows, so `@resolution` stays undefined. `resolution_units` then does `resolution unless defined?(@resolution)`, which calls `fetch` again. `test_instance_resolution_returns_nil_for_format_without_resolution` calls both on test.png and so fetches it twice, but passes.

The documentation says resolution returns nil when the image has no resolution data, but with raise_on_failure: true a valid GIF/WebP/PNG without pHYs raises CannotParseImage instead. `ImageBase#resolution` returns nil, so `parse_packets` does `raise CannotParseImage`, and `fetch` re-raises it with `raise if @options[:raise_on_failure]`. The comment says "Returns nil if the image does not contain resolution information". No test exercises resolution with raise_on_failure.

Resolution values have inconsistent numeric types: EXIF/TIFF paths return Floats and JFIF/PNG/BMP paths return Integers. The tests can't detect this because Ruby treats 72 == 72.0 as equal. Exif uses `num.to_f / den`, while JFIF uses `unpack("nn")` and PNG uses `unpack("NN")`. The fixtures mix `[[72, 72], :inches]` (test.jpg) and `[[72.0, 72.0], :inches]` (test2.jpg), and `assert_equal` passes either way, so the test doesn't pin the type.

Several unit-mapping branches the change adds are never exercised: JFIF centimeters, EXIF/TIFF centimeters and no-units, BMP with one zero axis, and JPEG EXIF-only resolution. A wrong mapping in any of them would pass the suite. The resolution expectations in GoodFixtures contain only :inches, :meters and :no_units (from JFIF and PNG). No fixture produces :centimeters, so the `JFIF_UNIT_CENTIMETERS` and `RESOLUTION_UNIT_CENTIMETERS` branches in jpeg.rb and tiff.rb are never run.

BMP pixels-per-metre values are read as signed and only rejected when both are zero, so negative or half-zero values (e.g. [[0, 2835], :meters]) are returned as valid resolution. `x_ppm, y_ppm = data[38, 8].unpack("l<l<")` followed by `return nil if x_ppm == 0 && y_ppm == 0`.
The change adds an unrelated editor-specific ignore entry that the resolution feature doesn't need. The diff adds `+.idea` to .gitignore. Nothing else in the change relates to IDE files.

Valid TIFF/EXIF layouts return no resolution when rational values precede the directory or share an offset. read_rational_resolution skips every offset behind the current stream position. An in-memory TIFF with XResolution and YResolution both pointing to the same 300/1 rational returned nil: reading X advances past the shared offset, so Y is skipped. A TIFF with separate 300/1 rationals before its IFD also returned nil.

A short JFIF segment raises an uncaught NoMethodError even with the default failure-handling options. An APP0 segment with length 7 and payload "JFIF\0" passes the identifier check, then data[7].ord raises NoMethodError. Calling FastImage.resolution with this in-memory JPEG reproduced the exception; FastImage#fetch does not rescue NoMethodError.

The new syntax prevents the library from loading on Ruby versions still allowed by the gem specification. fastimage.gemspec declares required_ruby_version >= 1.9.2, but Exif#initialize now uses keyword-argument syntax requiring Ruby 2.0, and jpeg.rb:51 uses safe navigation requiring Ruby 2.3. lib/fastimage/fastimage.rb unconditionally requires both parsers, so requiring fastimage on those older permitted runtimes fails with SyntaxError before any API can run.

The change makes /_emdash/api/search public and removes its permission check, but the endpoint still passes a caller-supplied `status` to the query, so anyone without a login can read the titles and text snippets of draft, scheduled or archived content. middleware/auth.ts adds "/_emdash/api/search" to PUBLIC_API_EXACT, and search/index.ts drops `requirePerm(user, "search:read")`. The handler then calls `searchWithDb(emdash.db, query.q, { collections, status: query.status, ... })`. schemas/search.ts declares `status: z.string().optional()`, and search/query.ts:219 filters on `AND c.status = ${status}`. The FTS triggers in fts-manager.ts index every row whatever its status. So `GET /_emdash/api/search?q=a&status=draft` with no session returns draft titles and snippets. The comment added in middleware/auth.ts:87-89 says "The query layer hardcodes status='published'". That is untrue, and it would lead a reviewer to skip this path.

Until setup is complete, the GitHub/Google OAuth callback makes any new OAuth user an ADMIN and then marks setup complete, so a stranger can take over a freshly deployed site and lock the owner out. The new `canSelfSignup` returns `{ allowed: true, role: Role.ADMIN }` whenever `emdash:setup_complete` is not true, before the allowed-domain check runs. After `handleOAuthCallback` it calls `finalizeSetup(emdash.db)`, which sets `emdash:setup_complete`. `/_emdash/api/auth/oauth/` is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES, and nothing links the callback to the setup wizard. Trigger: on a new install with GitHub OAuth configured, an attacker opens /_emdash/api/auth/oauth/github and finishes the GitHub login. They become admin and setup is marked complete. Before this change, the domain allowlist gated signup at this point.

Until setup is complete, the atproto callback gives ADMIN to whichever DID finishes OAuth first, including logins started from the public /atproto/login route. It never checks the handle the owner entered in the setup wizard, so an attacker who logs in first takes over the site and gets an account under the owner's email. `isFirstUser = setupComplete !== true && setupComplete !== "true"`, and then `findOrCreateOAuthUser(..., async () => { if (isFirstUser) return { allowed: true, role: Role.ADMIN }; ...})`. setup-admin.ts stores `handle: body.handle` in setup_state, but callback.ts never compares it with `atprotoSession.did`. For the first user it sets `email = setupState?.email` and `emailVerified: isFirstUser`. login.ts (under the public prefix `/_emdash/api/auth/atproto/`) has no setup-state check. Trigger: the owner completes wizard step 1; an attacker POSTs `{handle:"attacker.bsky.social"}` to /_emdash/api/auth/atproto/login and completes OAuth. They become admin, finalizeSetup runs, and the owner's setup flow then fails with SETUP_COMPLETE.

Comments in both OAuth callbacks claim that checking the setup_complete flag prevents a race that creates two admins. It doesn't: two concurrent callbacks can both read false and both create ADMIN users. callback.ts:126 says "Using an option flag instead of countUsers() avoids a TOCTOU race where two concurrent callbacks both see 0 users and both create admins". But the flag is read with `options.get("emdash:setup_complete")` and only written later by `finalizeSetup`, with no lock or conditional write in between. The core OAuth callback ([provider]/callback.ts:140) has the same comment and the same read-then-write pattern. The comment at line 147 even says "safe if two callbacks race past the check".

The integration now sets Astro's `security.checkOrigin: false` for the whole site, which removes Astro's built-in CSRF origin check from the user's own pages, form endpoints and actions outside /_emdash. EmDash's replacement check only covers /_emdash public and plugin API routes. `const securityConfig = { checkOrigin: false, ... }; updateConfig({ security: securityConfig, ...})`. `checkPublicCsrf` is called only from middleware/auth.ts for `isPublicApiRoute` and `/_emdash/api/plugins/`. The other /_emdash routes need the X-EmDash-Request header. Template or user routes such as a contact-form POST no longer get any origin check. This weakens a secure default.

A plugin whose allowedHosts contains "*" can now fetch any host, including localhost, private IPs and cloud metadata endpoints. The restricted HTTP client runs no SSRF validation, so this wildcard grants more than the `network:fetch:any` capability does. `isHostAllowed` gains `if (pattern === "*") return true;`. `createHttpAccess` only calls `isHostAllowed` and then `globalThis.fetch(currentUrl, ...)`. `createUnrestrictedHttpAccess` (the fetch:any path) calls `validateExternalUrl(currentUrl)` on every hop. Trigger: a plugin with `allowedHosts: ["*"]` calls `ctx.http.fetch("http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/")`, and the request goes through.

The atproto routes build client_id and redirect_uri from the internal request origin rather than the public origin this same change adds, so atproto login may fail behind a TLS-terminating proxy. The metadata document would also advertise whatever Host the request came in on. login.ts, setup-admin.ts:56 and callback.ts:42 all use `const baseUrl = url.origin;`. client-metadata.ts uses `new URL(request.url).origin`. Every core auth route in the diff was switched to `getPublicOrigin(url, emdash?.config)` for exactly this reverse-proxy case (see public-url.ts). Behind a proxy, `http://localhost:4321/_emdash/api/auth/atproto/callback` would be registered as the redirect_uri.

The atproto callback may allow login CSRF: it accepts any valid state/code pair without checking that the browser completing the flow is the one that started it, so an attacker could log a victim into the attacker's account. login.ts returns the authorize URL and sets no cookie or session marker. The OAuth state is held only server-side in the `auth:atproto` `states` collection (db-store.ts). callback.ts calls `client.callback(url.searchParams)` and then `session.set("user", { id: user.id })`, with no check that ties the state to the current session.

A new `pull_request_target` workflow with `pull-requests: write` runs a third-party action pinned to a mutable prerelease tag. Every other action in the repo is pinned by SHA, so a moved tag would run new code with a write token. `- uses: lunariajs/action@v1-prerelease` under `on: pull_request_target` with `permissions: pull-requests: write`. In the same diff, other actions use pinned SHAs (e.g. `actions/checkout@de0fac2e...`).

A new root devDependency installs from a pkg.pr.new preview build of an upstream pull request rather than a published, vetted release. It runs in CI (including the pull_request_target Lunaria job) and in the Docker build. `"@lunariajs/core": "https://pkg.pr.new/lunariajs/lunaria/@lunariajs/core@83617cc"`, with a matching tarball resolution in pnpm-lock.yaml:3007. i18n/build.ts and lunaria.config.ts import it.

The per-collection sitemap builds URLs from the internal request origin, while the sitemap index uses the public origin, so behind a proxy the child sitemaps list http://localhost URLs. sitemap-[collection].xml.ts: `const siteUrl = (settings.url || url.origin)`. sitemap.xml.ts and robots.txt.ts in the same diff use `settings.url || getPublicOrigin(url, emdash?.config)`.

The `search:read` permission check is removed from the suggest endpoint, which stays non-public, so any authenticated role can now call it. This looks unintended. The diff deletes `const denied = requirePerm(user, "search:read"); if (denied) return denied;` from suggest.ts. `/_emdash/api/search/suggest` is not added to PUBLIC_API_EXACT, so middleware still requires a login, but nothing checks the permission any more.

The admin CSP's img-src is widened from self plus the marketplace origin to any https origin, so injected markup in the admin can now load (and beacon to) arbitrary external images. `"img-src 'self' https: data: blob:"` replaces the earlier `buildEmDashCsp(marketplaceUrl)`, which allowed only 'self', data:, blob: and the marketplace origin.

Migration 034 uses a bare CREATE INDEX, while this same change patches 033 to IF NOT EXISTS for idempotency. A table that already has the index (e.g. a partial earlier run) would make the migration fail. 034: `CREATE INDEX ${sql.ref(`idx_${table.name}_deleted_published_id`)}`. 033 was edited in this diff from `CREATE INDEX` to `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` for every index. Editing the already-shipped migration 033 also changes history that existing databases have already run.

The new runtime image runs the Node server as root. The final stage `FROM node:22-slim` ... `CMD ["node", "./dist/server/entry.mjs"]` has no `USER` directive, so the server and the writable `data`/`uploads` directories are owned by root.

The changelog documents a `passkeyPublicOrigin` option that the code doesn't provide; the shipped option is `siteUrl`. The CHANGELOG entry says "Adds `passkeyPublicOrigin` on `emdash()`". runtime.ts:294 says siteUrl "Replaces `passkeyPublicOrigin`", and no code reads `passkeyPublicOrigin`.

The bonk action's pinned SHA changed but its version comment still gives the old date, so the pin can't be traced to a reviewed upstream revision. `ask-bonk/ask-bonk/github@c39e982d... # main 2026-03-23` became `ask-bonk/ask-bonk/github@7e200bbf... # main 2026-03-23`. The comment is unchanged.

The new atproto provider has no tests for its security-critical callback: the first-user admin grant, the allowlist and handle verification, and disabled-user rejection are all untested. The tests added for auth-atproto are auth.test.ts (descriptor shape), oauth-client.test.ts and resolve-handle.test.ts. None of them exercise routes/callback.ts or routes/login.ts.

Concurrent setup callbacks can link a second person's AT Protocol account to the initial administrator account. Two callbacks for different DIDs can both read setup_complete as false at lines 130–131. Both then use the setup wizard's email and set emailVerified=true. If the second callback reaches findOrCreateOAuthUser after the first creates the user, that function finds the same email and automatically links the second DID to the administrator. Neither the flag read nor account creation is protected by an atomic setup claim; finalizeSetup runs only afterward.

AT Protocol login and setup generate incorrect OAuth URLs behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy. When request.url has an internal origin such as http://localhost:4321 while config.siteUrl specifies the public HTTPS origin, login.ts passes url.origin directly to getAtprotoOAuthClient. That client constructs client_id and redirect_uris from this internal address and treats localhost as a loopback client. setup-admin.ts and callback.ts use the same internal-origin calculation, and client-metadata.ts also advertises it. None uses the change's getPublicOrigin helper, so the browser or PDS receives internal URLs instead of the configured public URLs.

The new palette-name text field probably can't take ordinary typing: the app's single-key shortcuts with no modifier keys (h, p, and now c) are likely to fire while the field has focus. Typing 'h' would hide the palette drawer and the field with it, so names containing those letters can't be entered. NavigationMenu has hidden buttons with `.keyboardShortcut("h", modifiers: [])`, `("p", modifiers: [])` and the new `.keyboardShortcut("c", modifiers: [])`. The 'h' button runs `historyDrawerVisible.toggle()`, and ColorHistoryDrawer, which holds PaletteNameField, only renders when `historyDrawerVisible` is true (ContentView). The builder added a first-responder check (`responder is NSTextView || responder is NSTextField`) only to the arrow/delete NSEvent monitor in AppDelegate.swift:98. Nothing stops these key equivalents while PaletteNameField's TextField (ColorHistoryDrawer.swift, `.focused($isFocused)`) is focused.

Deleting a named palette that sits before the selected one silently switches the selection to a different palette, because the selection is stored as an array index. `deletePalette(at:)` runs `palettes.remove(at: index)` and only resets `activePaletteIndex` when `>= palettes.count`. Example: palettes [History, A, B, C] with B selected (index 2). Deleting A gives [History, B, C], and index 2 now points at C. `renamingIndex` in PaletteTabBar is index-based in the same way.

Deleting a user-created palette is permanent and happens on a single context-menu click, with no confirmation and no undo. Clearing history got a confirmation in this same change. The context menu's `Button(PikaText.textPaletteDelete) { eyedroppers.deletePalette(at: index) }` calls straight into `palettes.remove(at:)`. By contrast, clear-history now goes through `isShowingClearConfirm` and an `.alert`. The undo/redo stacks (`undoStack: [[ColorPair]]`) only snapshot `autoHistory`, so a deleted palette can't be restored.

Undo/redo only covers the auto-history palette, so changes to saved palettes can't be undone: swapping, adding or removing a chip, and deleting a palette. ⌘Z after pressing X on a named palette restores the colours but leaves the saved chip swapped. `swap()` calls `pushUndo()`, which snapshots `autoHistory` only, then writes the swapped pair into `palettes[paletteIndex]` for whichever palette is active. `undo()`/`redo()` restore only `autoHistory = snapshot`. `addCurrentToPalette`, `deleteChipFromPalette` and `deletePalette` never call `pushUndo`.

The one-time migration moves the history to a new key and empties the old one, with no backup. Downgrading to an earlier build would show an empty history. `migrateHistoryToPalettes()` writes `Defaults[.palettes] = [history]` and then `Defaults[.colorHistory] = []`. The old key is cleared rather than left in place, and no test covers the migration.

Clicking the swap button now turns the icon twice (360°), so it lands back where it started instead of flipping 180°. `swapButton`'s action is `{ onSwap(); angle -= 180 }`. ContentView's `onSwap` sends `triggerSwap`, which posts `.triggerSwap` synchronously, and the newly added `.onReceive(... .triggerSwap) { _ in angle -= 180 }` subtracts another 180.

The new palette and compliance strings, and the reworded 'Toggle palettes', were added only in English. The other seven localisations will show raw keys such as 'palette.new', and the alert buttons are hard-coded English. A search for `palette.`/`compliance.toggle` finds them only in en.lproj. de, es, fr, hr, pl, zh-Hans and zh-Hant have only the old `history.toggle`/`history.clear` entries. ColorHistoryDrawer.swift:310 uses `Button("Clear", role: .destructive)` and `Button("Cancel", ...)` as literal strings.

Chips in a named palette still say 'Remove from history'. The palette-specific string that was added for them is never used. ColorHistoryChip always uses `Button(PikaText.textHistoryRemove, action: onRemove)`. `textPaletteRemoveChip` and `textPaletteNamePrompt` are declared in Constants.swift:216-217 and have no references anywhere.

If writing the export file fails, the error is silently discarded, so the user thinks the palette was saved when it wasn't. `try? json.write(to: url, atomically: true, encoding: .utf8)` follows `savePanel.runModal() == .OK` with no error handling or user feedback.

The compliance toggle icon never changes with its state, because both branches of the conditional are the same. `IconImage(name: showCompliance ? "checkmark.shield" : "checkmark.shield")`. The neighbouring preview toggle switches between `"eye"` and `"eye.slash"`.

Export creates a new ISO8601DateFormatter for every colour pair, and the change adds an `import Defaults` to Exporter that nothing uses. Inside `pairs.map`: `entry["date"] = ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: pair.date)`. Exporter.swift's new `import Defaults` is never used in that file.

The new palettes, the migration, the compliance toggle and the export JSON have no tests, so nothing checks the index handling or the migration result. PikaTests only has colour-conversion, compliance-algorithm and NotificationNames tests. Searching PikaTests for `toggleCompliance`, `savePalette` or palette names finds nothing, and the diff adds no test files.

The change includes visual and layout tweaks the palette feature doesn't need, which widens what has to be reviewed and regression-checked. SwapButtonStyle and ColorPreview animation durations go from 0.4 to 0.3. The `guard targetMode != displayMode` is removed. `.clipped()` is removed in ColorPickers.swift and `.clipShape` in PreviewPill. `.stroke` becomes `.strokeBorder`. The WindowCoordinator minimum and ideal height go from 260 to 280.

The New palette menu action does nothing when the palettes drawer is closed. NavigationMenuItems posts .savePalette, but its only receiver is PaletteTabBar.onReceive. ContentView creates ColorHistoryDrawer, and therefore PaletteTabBar, only when historyDrawerVisible is true. With the drawer closed, no receiver exists to execute the code that opens it.

Swapping a saved palette chip permanently changes it even after Undo restores the displayed colors. Select a chip in a named palette and invoke Swap: swap() calls pushUndo(), which snapshots only autoHistory, then replaces palettes[paletteIndex].pairs[index]. Undo restores only autoHistory and applies a history entry; it never restores the modified named palette chip.

Deleting a palette before the active palette silently switches selection to a different palette. With palettes [History, A, B, C] and B selected at index 2, deletePalette(at: 1) removes A but leaves activePaletteIndex equal to 2 because it is still below palettes.count. Index 2 now identifies C, so subsequent add, export, and delete-entry actions target C instead of B.

Setting `cancel-in-progress: true` on the Pages workflow means a second push to main cancels a run that is already in its `deploy` job, so a GitHub Pages deployment can be stopped part-way. The change also rewrites CI concurrency, which triage flagged as unplanned infra scope. The diff replaces `group: "pages"` / `cancel-in-progress: false` with `group: "pages-${{ github.ref }}"` / `cancel-in-progress: true`. The concurrency block is at workflow level (lines 25-27), so it covers the `deploy` job (`actions/deploy-pages@v4`, lines 57-70), which runs on every push to `refs/heads/main`. Two pushes to main in quick succession share the group `pages-refs/heads/main`, and the second cancels the first even while it is deploying. The old `false` value, GitHub's starter setting for Pages, let a running deployment finish and only skipped the queued runs in between. risk.json lists `infra` under `unplanned` with the match `.github/workflows/docs.yml`. Nothing else in the diff needs a workflow change: the rest is CSS.

In light mode, code blocks are forced onto a dark background with `!important` light-grey text. The syntax-highlighting theme loaded for light mode may still apply its own background and dark token colours to `code.hljs` and its spans, which would leave code samples, such as the C# block on the landing page, hard or impossible to read. Lines 232-239: `[data-bs-theme="light"] pre { background: #1e2530 !important; }` and `[data-bs-theme="light"] pre code { color: #e0ddd8 !important; }`. The stylesheet does not override `.hljs` backgrounds or any token colours (no `.hljs-*` rules). The light highlight themes the base `default`/`modern` templates may load set `.hljs { background: white }` and dark token colours (for example blue keywords). That would give light-grey text on a white `code` box, or dark-blue keywords on #1e2530. I could not see the base template's highlight theme in the export, so this is unverified.

The theme adds an unrequested runtime dependency on Google Fonts. Every docs visitor's browser now sends a request to fonts.googleapis.com/fonts.gstatic.com (a third-party privacy exposure), and the page's typography depends on an external, unpinned service. Line 9: `@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=IBM+Plex+Mono...&family=DM+Sans...&family=Outfit...&display=swap');`. Nothing in docfx.json or the repo vendors these fonts, and an `@import` at the top of the stylesheet also blocks rendering until the remote CSS loads.

In light mode, the amber link and inline-code colour on the off-white page background has a contrast ratio of about 2.9:1, below WCAG AA's 4.5:1. Links also have no underline, so readers with low vision or colour-vision deficiency may not be able to read or find links. Line 30: `--bs-link-color: var(--forge-ember)` with `--forge-ember: #e8760a` on `--bs-body-bg: var(--forge-white)` (#faf9f7), which works out to about 2.85:1 (hover colour #c4630a is about 3.9:1). Lines 365-369: `a { ... text-decoration: none; }`, so colour is the only cue. The same ember colour is used for inline code (`--bs-code-color`), landing `h3`s and `td strong`.

In dark mode, the navbar links, header buttons and footer text use #6b7280 on the #141a22 header/footer background, about 3.6:1 contrast, below WCAG AA's 4.5:1 for this small text. Line 59 in the dark block: `--forge-smoke: #6b7280`. Line 130: `.navbar .nav-link { font-size: 0.875rem; color: var(--forge-smoke) !important; }`. Lines 141-145 (`header .btn`) and 379-390 (`footer`, `footer .flex-fill`) also use `var(--forge-smoke)` on `var(--forge-anvil)` (#141a22).

The new palette gives ordinary links and dark-theme navigation insufficient text contrast, reducing accessibility for readers with low vision. Light-theme links use #e8760a against the #faf9f7 body background (2.84:1 contrast). In dark mode, .navbar .nav-link uses --forge-smoke (#6b7280) against the header's #141a22 background (3.62:1) at 0.875rem. Both fall below 4.5:1 for normal-sized text.

When `get()` lazily re-encrypts a record, it returns the credential with its old `version` even though the write-back has already bumped the stored version. Any caller that reads and then writes with CompareAndSwap gets a spurious VersionConflict, and if a CacheLayer sits above, the stale version stays cached. `get()` calls `self.inner.put(updated, PutMode::CompareAndSwap { expected_version: credential.version })` and discards the `Ok(_)` result, then does `Ok(credential)` with the original `version`. `InMemoryStore::put` sets `credential.version = expected_version + 1` on CAS, so the stored version is one higher than the returned one. `CacheLayer::get` (cache.rs:149-150) caches whatever the inner `get` returns. The new test `lazy_reencryption_on_read_when_key_id_differs` only checks the raw envelope's `key_id`. It never checks the returned version or a follow-up CAS write.

`with_keys` does not register the empty-string alias that `new()` adds for pre-rotation data. A deployment that moves from `new()` to `with_keys` for its first key rotation can no longer read any record that was never re-read (key_id ""). The crypto.rs doc also describes the opposite of what the code does. `new()` does `keys.insert(String::new(), key); // alias for pre-rotation data` (line 69). `with_keys` only collects the supplied pairs, so `key_for_id("")` returns `StoreError::Backend("encryption key '' not found — cannot decrypt")`. `EncryptedData.key_id` is `#[serde(default)]`, so old envelopes deserialize with "". crypto.rs:80 says "The encryption layer rejects empty key IDs at runtime", but `new()` accepts them. The public `encrypt()`/`encrypt_with_aad()` also still produce `key_id: ""`, while `encrypt_with_key_id` rejects it.

The no-AAD fallback was removed without any migration or detection path, so every record encrypted before AAD binding becomes unreadable through the layer after upgrade. The baseline test that guarded the old behaviour was rewritten to assert the opposite. The old `decrypt_data` fell back to `crypto::decrypt(key, &encrypted)` when AAD decryption failed. The new `decrypt_possibly_rotating` only calls `decrypt_with_aad` and maps any failure to `StoreError::Backend`. The test `legacy_data_without_aad_still_readable` (which asserted `fetched.data == b"legacy-secret"`) was renamed to `rejects_data_without_aad` and now asserts `unwrap_err()`. The crypto.rs doc says "a migration must re-encrypt all records before upgrading", but the diff contains no migration tool or command.

The persisted state identifiers and field names changed with no compatibility path. Stored records with state_kind "bearer", "basic_auth", "database_auth" or "header" now fail `KindMismatch`, and basic-auth JSON with a `username` field no longer deserializes into IdentityPassword (which expects `identity`). `identity_state!(BearerToken, "bearer", 1)` and `identity_state!(BasicAuth, "basic_auth", 1)` became `identity_state!(SecretToken, "secret_token", 1)` and `identity_state!(IdentityPassword, "identity_password", 1)`. The resolver rejects with `if stored.state_kind != expected_kind` (resolver.rs:243). The removed `BasicAuth` had `pub username: String`; `IdentityPassword` has `identity: String`. The only CredentialStore backend in the repo is InMemoryStore, so the impact today is limited.

The new Zeroizing return type is defeated straight away on the read path: the plaintext is moved into an ordinary Vec, and on rotation the whole credential (plaintext included) is cloned and dropped without zeroizing. `credential.data = std::mem::take(&mut *plaintext);` moves the bytes out of the `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` into `StoredCredential.data`. Then `StoredCredential { data: re_encrypted, ..credential.clone() }` clones `credential`, so its plaintext `data` is copied and then dropped without zeroization.

The change edits the CI toolchain pin, which the story did not cover (triage lists infra as unplanned). The edit looks like a fix, but it changes what the MSRV gate runs. `uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.100` became `@1.94`. The step is named "Install Rust 1.94", the job is "MSRV (1.94)", and Cargo.toml has `rust-version = "1.94"`, so the new value matches the declared MSRV. risk.json lists `"unplanned": ["infra"]`.

Both derive macros now expand to `::nebula_core::...` paths. A plugin crate that depends only on nebula-credential, as the macro's own doc example suggests, fails to compile with an unresolved `nebula_core`. The AuthScheme derive emits `impl ... ::nebula_core::AuthScheme` and `::nebula_core::AuthPattern::#pattern_ident`. credential.rs:123 now emits `<#scheme as ::nebula_core::AuthScheme>::pattern()`; the Credential derive previously used only `::nebula_credential` paths. The doc example in macros/src/lib.rs imports only `nebula_credential::AuthScheme`.

Patterns are categories shared by many types, not unique identifiers like the old `KIND`. Mismatch errors can now read "expected pattern SecretToken, got SecretToken", and the resolver parameter is still named and documented as `expected_kind`. `resolve_credential` passes `format!("{:?}", S::pattern())` as `expected_kind` to `CredentialResolverRef::resolve_scheme` (still documented as "expected_kind" at context.rs:37-39). `CredentialSnapshot::project` reports `expected: format!("{:?}", S::pattern())` and `actual: self.scheme_pattern`. Two distinct types with the same `AuthPattern` (for example, a plugin type using `pattern = SecretToken`) produce identical strings.

Lazy key rotation returns a stale record version, causing subsequent compare-and-swap updates to fail even without concurrent writers. When get() reads a record encrypted with an old key at version N, it writes the rotated ciphertext using CompareAndSwap { expected_version: credential.version }. InMemoryStore::put increments that version to N+1, but get() discards the returned record in Ok(_) and returns the original credential at version N. A caller using the returned version for its next CAS write therefore receives VersionConflict solely because of the read's rotation.

The encryption envelope documentation incorrectly says empty key IDs are rejected, obscuring the actual migration behavior. Receiving or sending a message after jumping into history skips intervening messages and disables loading them through loadNewer. With 100 chronological messages, jumpToMessage() targeting message 20 loads messages 10–30. If message 101 then arrives, appendNewMessage() calls pushMessage(), which appends 101 and synchronizes the newer cursor to it. syncCanLoadFlags() finds nothing after 101 and sets canLoadNewer=false, leaving messages 31–100 absent from the displayed window.

Programmatic jump scrolling cancels its own media correction lock, allowing subsequently loaded images to move the target out of position. scrollToMessageCenterWithRetry() sets jumpTargetId and a 1200ms lock, then scrollToMessageCenter() assigns container.scrollTop without updating lastScrollTop. The resulting scroll event enters onScroll(); any movement over eight pixels clears jumpTargetId and jumpLockUntil. onAnyMediaLoad() therefore cannot recenter that target when media subsequently changes the layout.
